text:
Before you start

You have Claude Code or Codex installed and signed in (Accounts and installation).
You can open a terminal, use cd to go into a folder, and start the agent there (Terminal survival kit).
Download the three example files. Each is one zip file:




Job
Download
What is inside




1. Organise a folder
messy-folder.zip
a folder messy-folder with 40 files


2. Clean a spreadsheet
messy-sheet.zip
messy-sheet.xlsx


3. Summarise PDFs
reports.zip
a folder reports with 6 short PDFs




Make a folder for this exercise, for example first-delegations in your Documents folder, and unzip the three files into it. On a Mac, double-click the zip. On Windows, right-click and choose Extract All. Windows sometimes puts the folder inside a folder of the same name; open it and make sure you can see the 40 files (or the 6 PDFs) directly.
Keep a short note open (a text file or paper) called what went wrong. Each time the agent does something you did not expect, write one line. We use these notes in the next unit.


Starting the agent in a copy
For every job, make a copy first and start the agent in the copy, never in the original.

In your file browser, duplicate the folder (for job 2, the folder holding messy-sheet.xlsx) and rename the copy, for example messy-folder-work.
In the terminal, go into the copy and start the agent:


Claude CodeCodex


cd ~/Documents/first-delegations/messy-folder-work
claude


cd ~/Documents/first-delegations/messy-folder-work
codex




If the agent asks whether you trust this folder, say yes: it is a copy of example data.
When the agent asks for permission to run a command or change files, read what it wants to do before you approve (Terminal survival kit). If you do not understand a command, ask: “What does this command do?”

title: Exercise: three small jobs
section: Worked example
text:
Worked example

Job 1: organise a messy folder
Make the copy messy-folder-work and start the agent in it. Before you type anything, open the folder in your file browser and look at it for a minute. Note how many items your file browser says there are.
Type this prompt (copy it, then change anything you would like differently):
This folder holds 40 files from a small lab project: data, images,
documents and slides. Organise it so that a colleague could find things.

What I want at the end:
- a few subfolders by kind of file (for example data, figures, documents)
- every file renamed as YYYY-MM-DD_short-description.ext, using the date
  in the name, or the file's own date if the name has none
- exact duplicates moved to a folder called duplicates, not deleted
- a file rename-log.csv with one row per file: old path, new path, reason
- nothing deleted, and nothing outside this folder touched

Before you move anything, show me your plan and list your assumptions,
for example how you read dates like 05-03-2024.
What to look for. The agent should first look at the files, then stop and show a plan and a list of assumptions. Read them. Do you agree with the folders? With how it reads the dates? If not, say so now. For example:
Use only three folders: data, figures, documents. Put the spreadsheets
in data. Otherwise go ahead.
Then let it work. It will ask before it creates folders and moves files.

Check the result

Count. In your file browser, count the files in each subfolder (the status bar or the folder’s info shows the number of items). The total, including duplicates, must be 40. Open rename-log.csv (in Excel or LibreOffice) and check it has 40 rows below the header.
Duplicates. There are exactly 3 exact duplicates (pairs of files with identical content), so 37 distinct files should be in the subfolders. Open each file in duplicates next to its twin. Are they really the same?
Tricky dates. Find these files in the rename log and check the new date:









Original name
Correct date
Why




data_05-03-2024 (1).csv
2024-03-05
a duplicate of data 2024-03-05.csv


Plate_reader_12.3.2024.csv
2024-03-12
day first


microscope 14-03-24.png
2024-03-14
there is no month 14


growth_curve_Mar26.csv
2024-03-26
the year is in the file’s date column


Meeting notes 4 March.txt
2024-03-04
the year is in the first line of the file


TODO (old).txt
2024-03-02
no date in the name; the file’s own date




Spot check. Pick three other rows of the log at random. Find the new file and open it. Is it the file the log says it is?
Not duplicates. fig2_final.png and fig2_final_REALLYfinal.png look like copies but are different figures. The same holds for the two survey_results files and the three lab protocols. None of them should be in duplicates.

If your file dates all show today’s date, your unzip tool did not keep the original dates. Then the agent has to use the contents of the files or ask you. That is fine, and a good thing to note in your what went wrong list.






Expected outcome for job 1






40 files: 10 .csv, 12 .png, 5 .docx, 5 .pdf, 5 .txt, 1 .md, 2 .xlsx.
3 exact duplicates: data_05-03-2024 (1).csv (copy of data 2024-03-05.csv), Copy of temps_20240409.csv (copy of temps_20240409.csv) and IMG_0042 (1).png (copy of IMG_0042.png). Which file of each pair goes to duplicates is your choice; the log should say.
37 distinct files. With folders data / figures / documents you get, for example, 10 / 11 / 16 (if the spreadsheets go in data).
Files with no date in the name take the file’s own date, for example logo.png 2024-01-15, figure1.png 2024-03-20, Report_final_v2.docx 2024-04-12.




Undo test (optional). Ask the agent: “Using rename-log.csv, put every file back where it was, with its old name. Then tell me how many files are in the folder.” You should be back at 40 files with the original names. Then ask it to redo the organisation, or simply make a fresh copy.



Job 2: clean a messy spreadsheet
Make a copy of the folder that holds messy-sheet.xlsx, start the agent in the copy, and open the sheet yourself in Excel or LibreOffice for a minute. What would you have to fix by hand?
messy-sheet.xlsx holds body weights from a mouse study. I want a tidy
table I can analyse, and a way to do the same next month.

What I want at the end:
- clean_weights.csv with one row per mouse and the columns animal_id,
  sex (F or M), group (control, low or high), dose_mg_per_kg,
  date_weighed (YYYY-MM-DD), weight_g (a number), comment
- a script that makes clean_weights.csv from the .xlsx file, so I can
  rerun it on a new sheet
- decisions.md: a numbered list of every decision you made, including
  each row you removed and how you read each odd value
Do not change messy-sheet.xlsx. If a value is unclear, leave it empty
and list it, rather than guess.
What to look for. The agent will probably write a short script in Python or R. To read Excel files it may need to install a package, and it will ask first. That is normal: approve it. If it asks which language you prefer and you have no preference, say Python.
When it is done, read decisions.md line by line. For each decision, ask yourself: would I have decided the same? Pay special attention to rows that were removed and to values that were changed.

Check the result
Open clean_weights.csv in Excel or LibreOffice. (If the weights look wrong, for example 241 instead of 24.1, that is your spreadsheet program’s regional setting, not the agent. Import it with Data → From Text/CSV and choose comma as separator and point as decimal, or ask the agent to also save the table as an .xlsx file.)

Rows. The sheet’s own note says “Total animals: 48”. The clean table must have 48 rows below the header: one per mouse, with B1-01 to B1-24 and B2-01 to B2-24.
Categories. Turn on the filter (Data → Filter) and open the drop-down of each column:

sex has only F and M: 26 F and 22 M.
group has only control, low and high, 16 mice each.
dose_mg_per_kg has only 0, 5 and 20, matching the groups.
date_weighed has exactly two dates: 2024-03-12 and 2024-04-09, 24 mice each. A third date means a day and month got swapped.

Total. Select the weight_g column. The status bar shows the average: it must be 23.27, the same as the Mean row in the original sheet. One weight is empty (B2-11, not weighed because the mouse was sick).
Spot check. Pick three mice at random, find them in the original sheet and compare every column. Some to try: B1-05 (male, low, 5, 2024-03-12, 24.1), B1-14 (female, control, 0, 2024-03-12, 17.5), B1-19 (male, low, 5, 2024-03-12, 23.7, re-weighed).
Rerun. Ask the agent: “Delete clean_weights.csv and run the script again. Is the new file identical to the old one?” A script you cannot rerun is not much use next month.

Now correct something. In many sessions at least one check fails the first time, often the dates. If one of yours fails, say exactly what is wrong. For example:
Row B2-17 has date 2024-09-04. Both weighings were in March and April
2024, so this must be 9 April; the sheet has it month first. Fix the
script, rerun it, and add this decision to decisions.md.
If every check passed, try a change of mind instead: “Put the comment about re-weighing in a separate column reweighed (yes/no). Update the script and decisions.md.” Then check that the rest of the table did not change.






Expected outcome for job 2





What had to happen to get from the sheet to 48 clean rows:

Rows 1 to 3 are headers (two of them with merged cells); row 3 holds the column names.
Below them are 55 rows: 48 mice, 1 duplicated row (B1-15 twice), 4 blank rows, 1 note row (“Batch 2 - arrived 2 April…”) and 1 Mean row.
Two IDs need tidying: B1-07 (trailing space) and b2-3 (meaning B2-03).
Sex is written as Female, female, F, f, F (with a space), Male, male, M and m.
Group is written as Control, control, ctrl, Ctrl, Low dose, low dose, LD, low, High dose, high-dose, HD and High.
Dose has units in some cells (5 mg/kg, 5mg/kg) and - or none for control animals, which means 0.
Weights have g in some cells, decimal commas in others (24,1), one 23.7 (re-weighed) and one not weighed (sick).
Dates are real Excel dates in some cells and text in others (12/03/2024, 12.3.2024, 12 March 2024). One cell, B2-17, is written month first: 04/09/2024 means 9 April 2024.

A full answer table is in messy-sheet-answer.csv (without the comment column). You can ask the agent to compare your table with it, but do your own checks first.






Job 3: summarise six PDFs into one table
Make a copy of the reports folder (for example reports-work) and start the agent in it.
This folder holds six short PDF reports. Make one table,
reports_summary.csv, with one row per report and these columns:
file, title, authors, date (YYYY-MM-DD), main_finding, one_line_summary,
and the page number where you found the title, the date and the
main finding.

Use only what is written in the reports. If something is missing or
unclear, write "not stated" and tell me; do not fill it in.
At the end, list every value you were unsure about.
What to look for. Claude Code can usually read PDFs directly. Codex usually runs a small program to extract the text, and may ask to install one. Either way, check the list of values the agent was unsure about at the end. A good answer mentions at least the date of the peer-feedback report and the date of the barley report.

Check the result

Rows. Six rows, one per PDF, no PDF missing.
Spot check three cells. Roll a die (or pick at random) for three cells. Open the PDF at the page the table names. Is the value there, and is it right?
The trap. Look at the main finding for the peer-feedback report. Is it this study’s own result, or the earlier pilot mentioned in the background?
Dates. Check the three hard ones yourself: the peer-feedback date (03/09/2025), the barley report (only a month) and the corrosion report (no date on page 1).
Correct. If something is wrong, say what is wrong, with the page: “The date of the corrosion report is on page 2: ‘Submitted 3 February 2025’. Fix the row and the page column.”







Expected outcome for job 3















File
Title (p. 1)
Authors
Date (page)
Main finding (page)




report-flipped-chemistry.pdf
Flipped classroom pilot in first-year chemistry
Lena Bergqvist, Omar Haddad
2025-03-14 (p. 1)
Exam pass rate rose from 61% (2024, 142 students) to 72% (2025, 138 students); attendance fell (p. 2)


report-soil-sensors.pdf
Soil moisture sensors in three urban allotments
Priya Natarajan
2025-06-30 (p. 1)
Low-cost sensors read 4.1 percentage points higher than the gravimetric reference; error grew above about 35% water content (p. 2)


report-peer-feedback.pdf
Peer feedback on lab reports in a molecular biology course
Henrik Sjöström, Maja Lindgren, Tomás Ruiz
2025-09-03 (p. 1)
No clear difference in report grades (mean 3.9 with vs 3.8 without peer feedback); students valued it (p. 2)


report-barley-drought.pdf
Drought tolerance of six barley lines in a greenhouse trial
Aino Virtanen
November 2024: no day stated (p. 1)
Line HB-17 kept 82% of its control biomass; the others 55-68% (p. 3, table)


report-hand-hygiene.pdf
Hand-hygiene reminders on a surgical ward: a before-and-after audit
Grace Okafor, Daniel Weiss
2025-01-22 (p. 1)
Compliance rose from 64% (410 opportunities) to 79% (395 opportunities) (p. 1, key finding box)


report-printed-steel.pdf
Corrosion of 3D-printed stainless steel coupons in seawater
Mateo Fernández
2025-02-03 (p. 2, “Submitted”)
Printed coupons lost about twice the mass of machined ones (0.42 vs 0.20 mg/cm²); heat treatment cut this to 0.27 (p. 2)



Notes:

Peer feedback, date. 03/09/2025 can be 3 September or 9 March. The report says it was written “in the first week of the autumn term”, after a course in spring 2025, so 3 September is right. A good agent flags this.
Peer feedback, finding. “Improved report grades by a full grade step” is another department’s pilot (p. 1), not this study’s result.
Barley, date. Only a month is given. “2024-11” or “not stated” (with a note) are both fine. “2024-11-01” is an invented day.
Corrosion, date. Page 1 has no date. The table should say page 2.
The one-line summaries will differ from person to person. Check that each one matches the report’s own conclusion.

title: Exercise: three small jobs
section: Try it on something of yours
text:
Try it on something of yours
You choose your own project at the end of Part 1, after Privacy, ethics and safety. Until then, only use files that are already public and contain no personal data.
If you want to try now, one safe option is a folder with 4-6 of your own published papers (open-access PDFs). Use the job 3 prompt to make a summary table, then check it: you know these papers better than anyone. Do not use student data, patient data, unpublished manuscripts, reviews, emails or anything from a shared drive.

title: Exercise: three small jobs
section: What you should have now
text:
What you should have now

messy-folder-work: an organised folder and a rename-log.csv that can undo it.
A folder with clean_weights.csv, the cleaning script and decisions.md.
reports_summary.csv with page references.
A record of your checks: which counts, totals and spot checks you did, and what they showed.
Your what went wrong list: every surprise, misread date or invented value. Bring it to the next unit, How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail, where we explain why these things happen.
The five-step checklist: copy, describe, record, check, correct. You will use it in every unit from now on.

section: Before you start
text:
Before you start

About 30–60 minutes, longer on a university-managed laptop.
An internet connection that is not blocked for claude.ai / chatgpt.com.
Your computer’s operating system: Windows 10 (version 1809 or later) or 11, macOS 13 or later, or a recent Linux (for example Ubuntu 20.04 or later). 4 GB of memory or more.
You do not need administrator rights for the installers. On a managed laptop, see When it does not work.
Nothing else. Git, R, Python and Quarto come later, with the agent’s help.


Accounts and licences
We give pointers, not prices: plans change often. Read the official pages.



Tool
What you need
Where




Claude Code
A paid Claude plan: Pro or higher (Max, Team, Enterprise). The free plan does not include Claude Code. Alternative: pay-as-you-go API billing through the Claude Console.
claude.com/pricing · Claude Code setup docs · Claude Console


Codex
A ChatGPT account. Codex is included across ChatGPT plans, including Free and Go, but with low limits, and on those plans terminal access may be limited. Plus or higher (Pro, Business, Edu, Enterprise) is realistic for the course. Alternative: an OpenAI API key, billed per use.
chatgpt.com/pricing · Codex pricing · Codex help article


Institutional plans
Claude for Education, Claude Team/Enterprise and ChatGPT Edu/Enterprise may include the agents. It depends on the institution’s workspace settings. Ask your IT department.
Local IT


GitHub
A free personal account. Educators can apply for GitHub Education benefits. Needed from Part 3; create it now.
github.com/signup · GitHub Education


Free software
Git, R (+ RStudio, optional), Python, Quarto. Not today: installed with the agent’s help in Terminal survival kit.
git-scm.com · cran.r-project.org · quarto.org









Subscription or API key?



Use a subscription (Claude Pro, ChatGPT Plus or an institutional plan) for this course. You pay a fixed amount and wait when you hit the limit. An API key bills per use, with no cap, which is easy to overspend while learning.

title: Exercise: accounts and installation
section: Worked example
text:
Worked example
Work through the steps in order. Do the steps for one tool first, get it working, and only then add the other if you want both.

Step 1: Get the accounts

Ask IT whether your university has a Claude or ChatGPT plan that includes Claude Code or Codex. A ready-to-send question: “Do we have a Claude or ChatGPT plan, and does it include Claude Code or Codex? If so, how do I get access?”
If not (or while you wait), get Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus yourself from the pricing pages above.
Create a GitHub account at github.com/signup. Choose a username you are happy to show colleagues: it becomes part of your project page address. Confirm the e-mail.

What you should see: you can log in at claude.ai and/or chatgpt.com in the browser, and your plan name is shown in the account settings. You can log in at github.com.


Step 2: Open a terminal
You only need it to paste a line today. Terminal survival kit explains it properly.

WindowsmacOSLinux



Press Win + X (the Windows key and X together).
Choose Terminal or Windows PowerShell. Not Command Prompt, and not an entry marked (x86).
You do not need Run as administrator.

What you should see: a window whose last line starts with PS, for example PS C:\Users\yourname>. If there is no PS, you are in Command Prompt: close it and try again.



Press Cmd + Space to open Spotlight.
Type Terminal and press Enter.

What you should see: a window whose last line ends with % or $, for example yourname@MacBook ~ %.



Press Ctrl + Alt + T, or search for Terminal in your application menu.

What you should see: a window whose last line ends with $, for example yourname@computer:~$.



Pasting: Ctrl + V or right-click in Windows Terminal/PowerShell; Cmd + V on macOS; Ctrl + Shift + V on Linux. Then press Enter.


Step 3: Install the agent
Copy the line for your system and your tool from this page (use the copy button at the right of each box), paste it into the terminal, and press Enter. The install may show no progress for a minute or two. Wait.

WindowsmacOSLinux


Claude Code (in PowerShell):
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
What you should see: after a short wait, a message that Claude Code was successfully installed. It may add Setup notes; read them.
Optional but recommended for Claude Code: Git for Windows. Without it, Claude Code uses PowerShell to run commands; with it, Claude Code can also use Bash. If you install it, accept all the default choices. You can also leave this until Terminal survival kit.
Codex (in PowerShell):
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1 | iex"
What you should see: progress lines starting with ==>, ending with a message that Codex is installed. It may ask whether to start Codex now; you can answer no and continue with Step 4.
Codex now runs natively on Windows. You do not need WSL (the Linux subsystem for Windows) for this course. If you already work in WSL 2, you can instead install both tools inside it with the Linux commands.






Already in Command Prompt (CMD)? Or prefer WinGet?





Claude Code in CMD:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.cmd -o install.cmd && install.cmd && del install.cmd
Claude Code with WinGet (does not update itself; run winget upgrade Anthropic.ClaudeCode now and then):
winget install Anthropic.ClaudeCode
Codex has no CMD line: use PowerShell.





Claude Code:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
What you should see: after a short wait, Claude Code successfully installed!, possibly with Setup notes about your PATH. Read them.
Codex:
curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh
What you should see: progress lines starting with ==>, ending with a note to open a new terminal and run codex. It may ask whether to start Codex now; you can answer no.






Already use Homebrew?





If you already use Homebrew, these work too. Homebrew installs do not update themselves; see Keep it up to date.
brew install --cask claude-code
brew install --cask codex





Claude Code:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
What you should see: after a short wait, Claude Code successfully installed!, possibly with Setup notes about your PATH. Read them.
Codex:
curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh
What you should see: progress lines starting with ==>, ending with a note to open a new terminal and run codex.
If curl is missing (curl: command not found), install it with your package manager first (for example sudo apt install curl on Ubuntu), or ask IT. Claude Code also offers signed apt, dnf and apk repositories; see the setup docs.









Only paste install lines from official sources



The address in the line must be claude.ai (Claude Code) or chatgpt.com (Codex). Copy from this page or the official docs, never from a forum post, video comment or e-mail.








Installing with npm instead





Both tools are also on npm: npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@latest (needs Node.js 22 or later) and npm install -g @openai/codex (needs Node.js). Use this only if you already work with Node.js. Never use sudo with these commands.





Step 4: Check that the terminal finds it

Close the terminal window and open a new one (Step 2). A window that was open during the install may not find the new program.
Type the version command for each tool you installed and press Enter:

claude --version
codex --version
What you should see: a version number, for example 2.1.330 (Claude Code) or codex-cli 0.171.0. Yours will be higher. If you instead see command not found or is not recognized, go to When it does not work.
For Claude Code, claude doctor gives a fuller health check of the installation.


Step 5: Make an empty folder and start the agent there
We use a new folder called agent-hello in your home folder, so the agent has nothing of yours to touch. Type these lines one at a time (they work on Windows PowerShell, macOS and Linux):
mkdir ~/agent-hello
cd ~/agent-hello
What you should see: after mkdir, nothing on macOS and Linux (that means success) or a short listing of the new folder on Windows; after cd, the prompt now mentions agent-hello.
Now start the agent:

Claude CodeCodex


claude
The first time:

It may ask a few setup questions, such as a colour theme. Any choice is fine.
It asks how to log in. Choose your Claude account with subscription (or the Console account if you use API billing).
A browser window opens. Log in with the account that has your plan, and approve.
Back in the terminal it confirms you are logged in. It may ask whether you trust the files in this folder. For your empty agent-hello folder, answer yes.

If no browser opens, press c to copy the login link, and paste it into your browser yourself. If the browser asks for a code to paste back into the terminal, copy all of it.
What you should see: a welcome box showing the version, the model, and the folder (ending in agent-hello), and a prompt where you can type.


codex
The first time:

Choose Sign in with ChatGPT.
A browser window opens. Log in with the ChatGPT account that has your plan, and approve.
Back in the terminal, Codex may ask whether you trust this folder or how much it may do without asking. For your empty agent-hello folder, accept the suggested default. (Codex can start in a read-only mode in folders that are not under version control. That is fine today; it will ask before writing.)
On Windows, Codex may ask to set up its sandbox (the protection that keeps it inside your folder). Accept the default. If it needs administrator approval you do not have, see When it does not work.

You can also sign in separately with codex login before you start.
What you should see: a short header with the model and the folder (ending in agent-hello), and a prompt where you can type.





Step 6: Say hello
Type each prompt below, press Enter, and read the answer before you type the next. Your answers will be worded differently from anyone else’s: agents are not deterministic.
Prompt 1. Ask it to look, not guess:
Which folder are we in, and what files can you see here?
What to look for: it should run a small action to list the files (you see a line saying it is listing or reading the folder) and then tell you the folder is empty. You know the right answer, because you just made the folder. If it claims to see files, you started it in the wrong folder (check the path it names), or it is guessing.
Prompt 2. A first small change. Replace the part in brackets with your own field (one general sentence, nothing confidential):
Create a file called hello.txt containing one sentence that says
I work in [your field]. Then tell me exactly what you did.
What to look for: the agent asks permission before it creates the file. Read the question. It should name hello.txt in your agent-hello folder. Choose Yes (the first option). Terminal survival kit explains the other options.
Prompt 3. Ask about its limits:
What can you do for me in this folder, and what would you ask
my permission for before doing it?
What to look for: a short, plain answer: it can read and write files here and run commands, and it asks before changing files or running commands (depending on settings). Keep this answer in mind for the next unit, where we test it.
Then leave the agent:









Claude Code
Codex




Leave
/exit (or Ctrl + D twice)
/exit or /quit (or Ctrl + C)


Stop it in the middle of an answer
Esc
Esc


See commands
/help
type /


Continue the last conversation in this folder
claude -c
codex resume




Check the result
“It replied” is not a check. Do all of these:

The file is really there. Open the folder in your normal file browser from the terminal: explorer . (Windows), open . (macOS) or xdg-open . (Linux). You should see hello.txt. Open it: it contains your sentence, and nothing else.
The agent did only what you asked. The folder contains hello.txt and nothing more. (Hidden settings files are fine; your file browser normally does not show them.)
Start and resume works. Start the agent again in the same folder with claude -c or codex resume and ask:
What did we do in our last conversation?
It should mention creating hello.txt. Then leave again.
Version check works in a fresh window. Close the terminal, open a new one, and run claude --version / codex --version once more.

If you installed both tools, repeat Steps 5–6 with the other one in the same folder, and compare: did both list the folder before answering? Did both ask before creating the file?



Keep it up to date
Both tools release new versions every week or so. When the course and your screen disagree, update first.








Installed with
Claude Code
Codex




Official installer (this page)
Updates itself in the background. Update now: claude update
codex update, or run the install line from Step 3 again


Homebrew
brew upgrade claude-code
brew upgrade --cask codex


WinGet
winget upgrade Anthropic.ClaudeCode



npm
npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code@latest
npm install -g @openai/codex





Desktop apps and editor extensions
Both tools also exist as a desktop app (Claude desktop app; the ChatGPT desktop app, which includes Codex) and as editor extensions (for example VS Code). They use the same engine. The course uses the terminal version because it is the same on every system. The desktop app is a good fallback if the terminal install is blocked on your computer.

title: Exercise: accounts and installation
section: When it does not work
text:
When it does not work
Find your symptom. Read the last lines the terminal printed: they usually name the problem.








What you see
What it means
What to do




command not found: claude / codex, or 'claude' is not recognized
The program is installed, but this terminal does not know where
1. Open a new terminal window and try again. 2. Look for Setup notes in the install output and run the fix it prints. 3. Use the PATH fix below. 4. Only then reinstall.


'irm' is not recognized
You are in Command Prompt, not PowerShell
Open PowerShell (Win + X)


The token '&&' is not a valid statement separator
You pasted the CMD line into PowerShell
Use the PowerShell line


'bash' is not recognized or parameter name 'fsSL'
You pasted the macOS/Linux line on Windows
Use the Windows line


does not support 32-bit Windows
You opened Windows PowerShell (x86)
Open Windows PowerShell without (x86)


running scripts is disabled on this system
Windows script policy blocks the installer
On a managed laptop, ask IT. Do not change the policy yourself on a work computer.


syntax error near unexpected token '<', HTML in the terminal, or 403
The install address returned a web page instead of the script: blocked network, region, or a temporary error
Try once more. If it repeats, check the page text: “App unavailable in region” means the service is not offered in your country. On a university network, ask IT.


Certificate, SSL/TLS or unable to get local issuer certificate errors
A university or company network inspects encrypted traffic
Ask IT; send them the exact error and the official install page


Claude Code says your account has no access
You logged in with a free Claude account, or a workspace where Claude Code is switched off
Check the plan at claude.ai. Use /login inside Claude Code to switch account.


Wrong account is used
The browser remembered another login (personal vs university)
Log out in the browser, then /login (Claude Code) or /logout and start again (Codex)


No browser opens at sign-in
The terminal cannot open a browser
Claude Code: press c to copy the link, paste it into a browser. Codex: copy the link it prints.


The agent lists your other files
You started it in the wrong folder
/exit, then cd ~/agent-hello, then start again




The PATH fix
Only if a new terminal still cannot find claude or codex, and the install output did not print a fix you could follow. Both installers put the program in a folder called .local/bin in your home folder (on Windows, %USERPROFILE%\.local\bin for Claude Code). These commands add that folder to the list the terminal searches. You only do this once.

WindowsmacOSLinux


In PowerShell, check that the file exists:
Test-Path "$env:USERPROFILE\.local\bin\claude.exe"
If it prints True, add the folder to your PATH:
$currentPath = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', 'User')
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable('PATH', "$currentPath;$env:USERPROFILE\.local\bin", 'User')
Close PowerShell, open a new one, and try claude --version. If it printed False, the install did not finish: run the install line again and read its output.
For Codex on Windows, the installer manages its own PATH entry. If codex is not found in a new window, run the install line again and read the last lines.


Check that the file exists:
ls -la ~/.local/bin/claude ~/.local/bin/codex
If it lists the files, add the folder to your PATH (zsh is the default shell on macOS):
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc
Then try claude --version again.


Check that the file exists:
ls -la ~/.local/bin/claude ~/.local/bin/codex
If it lists the files, add the folder to your PATH (bash is the default on most distributions):
echo 'export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
Then try claude --version again.





University-managed laptops

The installers do not need administrator rights: they install into your own user folder.
IT policy can still block scripts, downloads or the companies’ websites. Do not try to work around it. Send IT the exact error message and the links to the official install pages: Claude Code setup, Codex CLI.
Meanwhile, ask whether the desktop app is available in your software centre, or work on a personal computer for the course exercises (example data only, so no university data is involved).



Official troubleshooting pages

Claude Code: Troubleshoot installation and login · Terminal guide for new users
Codex: Codex CLI · Authentication · Windows sandbox · WSL

title: Exercise: accounts and installation
section: What you should have now

title: Accounts and installation
section: About this lecture
text:
About this lecture
You have seen what an agent can do. Before you can try it yourself, three things must be in place: an account that includes the agent, the agent program on your own computer, and one working conversation with it. This is the only unit where most of the work is setting things up, and it is the one where people most often get stuck. We go slowly.

Claude Code needs a paid Claude plan (Pro or higher) or API billing. Codex needs a ChatGPT account; Plus or higher is realistic.
Both are installed by pasting one line into a terminal. The terminal is just the place where you paste it.
The first start opens a browser window to sign in. After that, the agent runs in the terminal.
Your first conversation happens in an empty folder, so nothing of yours is at stake.

This is a practical unit. The exact commands live on the exercise page, which we update before each run. Using the terminal properly comes in Terminal survival kit.

Welcome to the unit everyone dreads a little: installation. The good news is that installing these tools has become much simpler. For each tool, it is one line pasted into a terminal, followed by a sign-in in the browser. The less good news is that every computer is slightly different, and university laptops in particular can have restrictions. So this unit is as much about what to do when it does not work as about the happy path. I will show you the shape of the process here. The exact commands, which change from time to time, are on the exercise page, and that page is the one you should have open when you actually install. We do not learn the terminal today. We only open it, paste, and press Enter. The next unit teaches the terminal properly.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Monday morning: you want to try this on a real task
text:
Monday morning: you want to try this on a real task
Imagine a teacher who saw the live build in Why agentic AI? and wants to try it on their own course material on Monday. Between them and the first useful result stand:

an account: which plan? Is the free one enough? Does the university already pay for something?
an install: on a laptop where they have never opened a terminal;
a sign-in: linking the program on the laptop to the account in the browser;
a first test: how do they know it works?

Each step is small. Missing any one of them stops everything. This lecture walks the path once, so that you recognise each step when you do it.


Let us make it concrete. Picture a colleague who wants to try this on Monday morning. They have perhaps used ChatGPT in a browser before. What stands between them and a working agent is not one big obstacle but four small ones in a row: account, install, sign-in, first test. Each takes a few minutes when it goes right. The trouble is that when one goes wrong, the error messages are written for programmers. So the plan for today is to walk the whole path once, slowly, and to look at the typical ways each step goes wrong. When you then do it yourself in the exercise, you will know where you are on this path at every moment.

title: Accounts and installation
section: You need three things: a plan, a program and a place to type
text:
You need three things: a plan, a program and a place to type



An account with a plan that includes the agent. This is where the AI model runs and how usage is paid for.
The agent program installed on your computer. It reads your files, runs commands and talks to the model over the internet.
A terminal to start the program and talk to it.

Each tool (Claude Code, Codex) needs its own account and its own program. The terminal is the same for both.




It helps to separate three things that are easy to mix up. First, the account. The language model itself runs on the company’s servers, not on your laptop, and your plan decides how much you may use it. Second, the program. This is a small application that sits on your computer, reads your files when you ask, runs commands, and sends your requests to the model. Third, the terminal, which is simply the window where you start the program and type to it. Claude Code and Codex each need their own account and their own program, but they share the terminal. When something fails later, it helps to ask which of the three is the problem: is it my account, my installation, or my terminal?

title: Accounts and installation
section: Claude Code needs a paid Claude plan; the free plan does not include it
text:
Claude Code needs a paid Claude plan; the free plan does not include it



Pro is the entry level that includes Claude Code. Max, Team and Enterprise include it too, with higher limits.
The free Claude plan does not include Claude Code.
Alternative: pay-as-you-go API billing through the Claude Console. You pay per use instead of per month.
Plans have usage limits that reset over time. Heavy days can hit them; the agent then tells you when you can continue.

We give no prices: they change. Links to the official plan pages are on the exercise page.




For Claude Code, the rule is simple. The free Claude plan, the one many of you may have used in the browser, does not include Claude Code. You need Pro or something above it: Max, Team or Enterprise. The other route is the Claude Console, where you buy API credits and pay for what you use. Every plan has usage limits that reset after some hours. On a normal day of course work, Pro is usually enough; if you use the agent for long sessions every day, you may hit the limit and have to wait. I am deliberately not giving prices, because they change between course runs. The exercise page links to the official pricing page.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Codex comes with a ChatGPT account; Plus or higher is realistic
text:
Codex comes with a ChatGPT account; Plus or higher is realistic

Codex is included across ChatGPT plans, including Free and Go, but with low limits there. On those plans, access to the terminal version may also be limited or still rolling out.
Plus or higher (Pro, Business, Edu, Enterprise) is what we recommend for the course.
You can also sign in with an OpenAI API key and pay per use, as with the Claude Console.
You sign in with the same account you use for ChatGPT in the browser.

Do you need both tools? For almost every unit, one is enough. Having both pays off in Parallel workers, where we compare them and let one review the other.

Codex is OpenAI’s agent, and it is tied to your ChatGPT account. OpenAI includes Codex in all ChatGPT plans, even the free ones, but the free tiers have low limits and OpenAI’s own pricing page currently lists them mainly for the desktop app. In practice, Plus or higher is what you want for this course. If you already pay for ChatGPT Plus, you already have Codex. As with Claude, there is also an API-key route where you pay per use. Do you need both? No. Every exercise gives instructions for both tools, and you can follow any of them with one. The Parallel workers unit later in the course is where having both really helps, so if you are curious, it is worth keeping the option open.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Your university may already pay for a plan: ask IT before you pay yourself
text:
Your university may already pay for a plan: ask IT before you pay yourself



Institutional plans exist: Claude for Education, Claude Team/Enterprise, ChatGPT Edu/Enterprise.
Whether they include Claude Code or Codex depends on the institution’s workspace settings. An administrator can switch these on or off.
An institutional plan can also come with better data terms (no training on your data). That matters in Privacy, ethics and safety.

Ask IT: “Do we have a Claude or ChatGPT plan, and does it include Claude Code or Codex?”




Before you pay out of your own pocket, find out whether your university already has an agreement. Many institutions now have Claude for Education, ChatGPT Edu or an enterprise plan. Having the plan is not the same as having the agent, though. The workspace administrator decides which features are switched on, and coding agents are sometimes switched off by default. So the question to send to IT is specific: do we have a plan, and does it include Claude Code or Codex? An institutional plan has one more advantage: the data terms are usually stricter, for example a promise not to train on your data. We come back to why that matters in the privacy unit.

title: Accounts and installation
section: A subscription has a monthly cap; an API key has a meter
text:
A subscription has a monthly cap; an API key has a meter





Subscription (Pro, Plus, …): a fixed monthly cost. When you reach the limit, you wait for it to reset. No surprise bills.
API key (Claude Console, OpenAI Platform): you pay per use. No waiting, but a long session can cost more than you expect.

For this course, use a subscription. It makes the cost predictable while you learn. An API key is for automation or for an institution that prefers usage billing.


There are two ways to pay, and it is worth understanding the difference. A subscription works like a gym card: a fixed monthly cost, and if you use it a lot, you hit a limit and have to wait a few hours. You never get a surprise bill. An API key works like a taxi meter: you pay for exactly what you use. That is good for automated jobs, but while you are learning, a long session where the agent reads many files can cost more than you would guess. So for this course we recommend a subscription. If your institution gives you an API key instead, that also works; just keep an eye on the usage page.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Create a free GitHub account now, even though we need it only in Part 3
text:
Create a free GitHub account now, even though we need it only in Part 3

GitHub is where we will store, share and publish projects (GitHub, A course or project page).
A free personal account is enough. Educators can apply for extra benefits through GitHub Education.
Create it now: choosing a username and confirming the e-mail takes a few minutes, and it is one less thing to do later.
Pick a username you are happy to show colleagues. It appears in the web address of your project pages.

You do not need to do anything on GitHub yet.

One more account, and it is free. GitHub is the website where code and projects are stored and shared, and in Part 3 we use it to publish your project page. You will not touch it until then, but creating an account takes a few minutes and sometimes involves waiting for an e-mail, so do it now while you are setting things up anyway. One practical tip: your username becomes part of the address of your published pages, something like username dot github dot io. Choose something you would be happy to put on a slide or a CV. Teachers can also apply for GitHub Education, which gives some extra features for free.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Git, R, Python and Quarto can wait: the agent will install them with you
text:
Git, R, Python and Quarto can wait: the agent will install them with you

Later units use free software: git (version history), R and Python (analysis), Quarto (web pages).
You do not install them today.
In Terminal survival kit we let the agent check what is already there and install what is missing, explaining each step before it runs it.
On a managed laptop, some of these may need to come from IT’s software centre instead. We will say where.


You may have heard that you need to install a long list of programs to do data analysis: R, Python, git, and so on. We will need some of them later, but not today. In fact, installing them is a good first task for the agent itself: it can check what you already have, suggest what is missing, and explain each command before it runs it. We do that in the next unit. If your laptop is managed by the university, some programs may have to come from the IT department’s software centre instead, and the agent can help you figure out which. Today, the only programs we install are the agents themselves.

title: Accounts and installation
section: The agent is a program on your computer, not a website
text:
The agent is a program on your computer, not a website


A chat runs in the browser. It sees only what you paste in.
An agent runs on your computer. It can read and change files in the folder where you start it, and run programs there.
That is why it must be installed, and why where you start it matters.


Here is why there is an install step at all. When you use ChatGPT or Claude in the browser, everything happens on a web page. The model sees only what you type or paste. A coding agent is different: it is a program that runs on your own computer, and it can open the files in a folder, write new files, and run programs such as R or Python. The thinking still happens on the company’s servers, but the hands are on your machine. That is what makes it useful, and it is also why we care so much about which folder you start it in. Today we start it in an empty folder, so it has nothing to touch.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Desktop apps and editor extensions exist; we use the terminal version because it is the same everywhere
text:
Desktop apps and editor extensions exist; we use the terminal version because it is the same everywhere


Both tools come in several forms:

a terminal program (Claude Code CLI, Codex CLI);
a desktop app (the Claude desktop app, the ChatGPT desktop app with Codex);
editor extensions (for example VS Code).

They share the same engine. The course uses the terminal version because it looks and works the same on Windows, macOS and Linux, and every feature appears there first.
The desktop app is a good fallback if the terminal install is blocked on your laptop.




You may wonder why we use the terminal at all, when both companies offer desktop apps with buttons and windows. The honest answer is consistency. The terminal version is the same on every operating system, so the instructions in this course work for everyone. Desktop apps change their menus often, and they differ between Windows and Mac. The terminal version also gets new features first, and it is the version the documentation describes. That said, the engine underneath is the same. If your laptop does not let you install the terminal version, the desktop app is a perfectly fine fallback, and most of what we teach carries over.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Opening a terminal takes one shortcut on each system
text:
Opening a terminal takes one shortcut on each system


macOS: Cmd + Space, type Terminal, press Enter.
Windows: Win + X, choose Terminal or Windows PowerShell.
Linux: Ctrl + Alt + T, or search for Terminal.


Now the practical part. To install, you need a terminal window. On a Mac, press Command and Space to open Spotlight, type Terminal and press Enter. On Windows, press the Windows key and X together, and choose Terminal or Windows PowerShell from the menu. On most Linux systems, Control, Alt and T opens one. In each case you get a window with some text and a blinking cursor. That is all we need today: a place to paste one line and press Enter. You do not need to understand what else is in the window yet; that is the next unit.

title: Accounts and installation
section: On Windows, check that the prompt starts with PS
text:
On Windows, check that the prompt starts with PS





Windows has two command windows: PowerShell and the older Command Prompt (CMD). They need different install commands.
PowerShell shows PS C:\Users\yourname>. CMD shows the same without PS.
Use PowerShell. Do not pick the entry marked (x86): that is the 32-bit version and the tools refuse to run in it.
You do not need “Run as administrator”.



Windows has a small trap. There are two kinds of command window: PowerShell, which is the modern one, and Command Prompt, also called CMD, which is older. They look almost the same, but they understand different commands, so an install line written for one fails in the other. The quick check is the start of the line: PowerShell puts the letters PS in front. Use PowerShell. If your Start menu also shows “Windows PowerShell (x86)”, avoid that one: it is the 32-bit version, and the tools do not run in it. And you do not need to run it as administrator. Both installers put the program in your own user folder.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Installing is one pasted line per tool
text:
Installing is one pasted line per tool

Paste the line, press Enter, wait. The download shows little or no progress. It ends with a message that the install succeeded, or with an error you can look up.

Here is what an installation looks like. You paste one line, press Enter, and wait. For Claude Code there is often no progress bar at all for a while, which makes people think it has hung. Give it a minute or two. At the end you get a message saying the installation succeeded, sometimes with a note about something called PATH, which we come to shortly. Codex’s installer behaves similarly, and it may offer to start Codex right away. Your screen will look slightly different from this picture: version numbers, colours and wording change. What matters is the last few lines: success, or an error message.

title: Accounts and installation
section: The install lines: one for macOS and Linux, one for Windows
text:
The install lines: one for macOS and Linux, one for Windows









macOS / Linux (Terminal)
Windows (PowerShell)




Claude Code
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh \| bash
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 \| iex


Codex
curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh \| sh
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1 \| iex"




These were the official commands when this deck was written. Copy them from the exercise page, which we check before each run.
Alternatives exist: Homebrew on macOS, WinGet on Windows, npm (needs Node.js). Use them only if you already know them.
Codex on Windows now runs natively in PowerShell. WSL (Linux inside Windows) also works for both tools but is not needed for this course.


Here are the actual lines, for orientation. Each tool has one line for Mac and Linux, and one for Windows PowerShell. Please do not type these off the slide: copy them from the exercise page, which we check before every course run, because these commands do change. There are also alternative routes. If you already use Homebrew on a Mac, or WinGet on Windows, or npm, both tools can be installed that way, but they then do not always update themselves. For a beginner, the official one-line installer is the simplest. A note for Windows users who have read older guides: Codex used to require WSL, the Linux subsystem for Windows. That is no longer the case; it now runs directly in PowerShell.

title: Accounts and installation
section: The install line downloads a program and tells the terminal where it is
text:
The install line downloads a program and tells the terminal where it is


Download a small script from the company’s site and run it.
The script puts the program in a folder in your home directory (often .local/bin).
It adds that folder to the PATH: the list of folders the terminal searches when you type a command name.

Then typing claude or codex starts the program.

It is worth knowing roughly what that one line does, because it explains the most common problem. First, it downloads a small installer script from the company’s website and runs it. Second, the script puts the actual program into a folder inside your home directory, typically a hidden folder called dot local slash bin. Third, it adds that folder to something called the PATH. The PATH is simply a list of folders where the terminal looks when you type the name of a program. If the folder is on the list, typing claude or codex starts the program. If it is not on the list, the terminal says it cannot find the command, even though the program is installed. Keep this picture in mind for the troubleshooting slides.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Pasting an install line means trusting where it comes from
text:
Pasting an install line means trusting where it comes from

The pattern “download a script and run it” is normal for these tools, and it gives that script your user’s rights.
Check the address: claude.ai for Claude Code, chatgpt.com for Codex.
Copy from the official documentation or the course page, never from a forum, a video comment or an e-mail.
If a page asks you to paste a command to “fix” something urgent, stop and ask.


A word of caution, because this is a habit worth building now. Pasting a line that downloads and runs a script is completely normal for these tools, and the official documentation tells you to do exactly that. But it means you are running whatever that script contains, with your own permissions. So check where it comes from. The address in the line should be claude dot ai for Claude Code and chatgpt dot com for Codex. Copy from the official docs or our exercise page. There are scams that ask people to paste a “fix” into their terminal; if anyone asks you to paste a command urgently, that is a reason to stop and ask a colleague.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Close the terminal and open a new one before you test
text:
Close the terminal and open a new one before you test





A terminal reads the PATH when it opens. A window that was open during the install may not know about the new program yet.
So: close the window, open a new one, then test.
If you use a terminal inside an editor (VS Code), restart the editor.



This one fixes more install problems than anything else. A terminal window reads the PATH list once, when it starts. If you install a program in that window, the installer updates the list for future windows, but the window you are in may still have the old list. So the very first thing to do after installing is: close the terminal window and open a new one. If you use a terminal inside an editor such as VS Code, close and reopen the whole editor, because it passes its own copy of the list to the terminals inside it.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Check the installation: the version command prints a number
text:
Check the installation: the version command prints a number
claude --version
2.1.330 (Claude Code)
codex --version
codex-cli 0.171.0

A version number means the program is installed and the terminal can find it.
Your numbers will be higher: both tools update often.
An error such as command not found or is not recognized means the terminal cannot find it yet. We fix that later in this lecture.


Now we check. In the new window, type claude, space, dash dash version, and press Enter. If you see a version number, the installation worked and the terminal can find it. Do the same for codex if you installed it. The numbers on the slide are just examples from when this deck was written; yours will be higher, because both tools release new versions very often, sometimes several times a week. If instead you get “command not found” or “is not recognized”, do not reinstall straight away. That almost always means the PATH problem from two slides ago, and we will fix it at the end of the lecture.

title: Accounts and installation
section: The first start opens your browser to sign in
text:
The first start opens your browser to sign in


Type claude (or codex) and press Enter. The first time, it asks how you want to sign in. Choose your subscription (Claude account / Sign in with ChatGPT).
A browser window opens. Log in as usual, approve, and go back to the terminal.
If no browser opens, the terminal shows a link (Claude Code: press c to copy it). Paste it into your browser.


The first time you start the agent, it does not know who you are. Type claude, or codex, and press Enter. It shows a short sign-in screen and asks which kind of account you have. Choose the subscription option: your Claude account for Claude Code, or Sign in with ChatGPT for Codex. Your web browser then opens a login page. Log in the way you always do, approve the request to connect, and switch back to the terminal window: it should now say you are signed in. Claude Code may also ask a couple of small questions first, such as which colour theme you prefer; any answer is fine. If no browser window opens, which can happen on locked-down machines, the terminal shows a long link you can copy into the browser yourself. The sign-in is remembered, so you do this once per computer.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Make an empty folder for your first conversation
text:
Make an empty folder for your first conversation





The agent works in the folder where you start it.
For the first test, make a new, empty folder, for example agent-hello in your home folder.
Start the agent inside that folder. The exercise page gives the two commands.
Not in your home folder, Desktop or Documents itself: those are full of your files.



Before we say hello, we decide where. The agent works in the folder where you start it: it can read what is there and, with your permission, change it. So for the very first conversation, we use a new, empty folder. In the exercise, you make one called agent-hello inside your home folder, move the terminal into it with one command, and start the agent there. Please do not start your first session in your home folder or on your Desktop. Those are full of your own files, and we have not yet talked about permissions. A habit we keep for the whole course: one project, one folder, and the agent starts there.

title: Accounts and installation
section: The first hello: ask the agent what it can see
text:
The first hello: ask the agent what it can see

The folder is empty, so a good answer says so. If it claims to see files, something is off: you started it in the wrong folder, or it is guessing.

And now the moment: your first conversation. Type a plain question, such as: which folder are we in, and what files can you see here? A good agent looks, rather than guesses. You will see it run a small action to list the files, and then it tells you the folder is empty. That is already a tiny verification exercise. You know the true answer, because you just made the folder. If it lists files, either you started it in the wrong folder, or it is making things up. Either way, you have learned something. Then ask it to create a small file, and approve when it asks. Finally, open the folder in your normal file browser and check that the file is really there.

title: Accounts and installation
section: The agent asks before it changes things; say yes for now, we discuss this next time
text:
The agent asks before it changes things; say yes for now, we discuss this next time



When the agent wants to create or change a file or run a command, it may stop and ask.
For the test file in your empty folder, choose Yes.
On first start, it may also ask whether you trust this folder. For your own empty folder: yes.
Reading these questions properly, and the different permission modes, is the core of Terminal survival kit.





When you ask the agent to create a file, it will probably pause and ask whether it may. This is the agent’s safety catch, and it is a good thing. Today, in an empty folder, with a file you asked for, the answer is yes. You might also be asked once whether you trust the folder; for your own empty test folder, that is fine too. Next unit we spend real time on these questions: how to read what the agent wants to do, what the options mean, and how to make it ask less or more. For today, the rule is: only say yes when you understand what it is asking and it is what you wanted.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Leave the agent with /exit; your conversation is saved
text:
Leave the agent with /exit; your conversation is saved









Claude Code
Codex




Leave
/exit, or Ctrl + D twice
/exit or /quit, or Ctrl + C


Stop it mid-answer
Esc
Esc


List commands
/help
type /


Continue the last conversation
claude -c
codex resume



Commands that start with / are instructions to the program, not to the AI.

A few practical keys, so you can get out again. Both tools understand commands starting with a slash; these go to the program itself rather than to the AI. Slash exit leaves. Escape stops the agent if it is in the middle of something you do not want. Your conversations are saved on your computer, and you can pick the last one up again with claude dash c, or codex resume. You do not need to memorise this table; it is on the exercise page, and the next unit uses these all the time.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Keep the tools up to date: Claude Code updates itself, Codex needs a nudge
text:
Keep the tools up to date: Claude Code updates itself, Codex needs a nudge


Claude Code (official installer)

Updates itself in the background; the new version is used next time you start it.
To update now: claude update.
Health check: claude doctor.

Codex

Update with codex update, or run the install line again.
Homebrew/npm installs update through those tools.





New versions arrive weekly or faster. When something in this course looks different on your screen, update first.


Both tools change quickly. New versions come out every week, sometimes several times. Claude Code, when installed with the official installer, updates itself in the background, and the new version starts next time you open it. If you want to update right away, type claude update in the terminal. Claude doctor gives you a quick health check of the installation. For Codex, either run codex update or simply run the install line again, which also updates. One rule for the course: if what you see on screen does not match the instructions, update first, then ask.

title: Accounts and installation
section: “Command not found” means the terminal cannot find the program yet
text:
“Command not found” means the terminal cannot find the program yet


Open a new terminal and try again. This fixes most cases.
Read the end of the install output: it often prints a “Setup notes” line with the exact fix.
Still not found: the program’s folder is not on the PATH. The exercise page gives the one-time fix for your system.
Only then reinstall.


Now, the most common failure: you type claude and the terminal answers “command not found”, or on Windows, “claude is not recognized”. In nine cases out of ten, the program is installed fine, and the terminal simply does not know where it is. First fix: close the terminal, open a new one, try again. Second: scroll up in the install output. The installer often notices the problem and prints the exact fix in a section called setup notes. Third, if that does not help, the exercise page has the one-time command that adds the folder to the PATH for your system. Reinstalling is the last resort, not the first, because it rarely fixes a PATH problem.

text:
Windows errors that mean “wrong kind of terminal”








What you see
What it means
Fix

Open PowerShell (Win + X)


The token '&&' is not a valid statement separator
You pasted the CMD line into PowerShell

On Windows, a whole family of errors means just one thing: the command and the window do not match. If you see “irm is not recognized”, you are in Command Prompt, not PowerShell. If you see a complaint about the token double ampersand, you pasted the Command Prompt version into PowerShell. If it complains about bash, or about a parameter called fsSL, you copied the Mac and Linux line by mistake. And the 32-bit message means you opened the x86 version of PowerShell. In every case the fix is to match the line to the window. None of these mean anything is broken.

title: Accounts and installation
section: On a university-managed laptop, the install may be blocked: ask IT, or use the desktop app
text:
On a university-managed laptop, the install may be blocked: ask IT, or use the desktop app





Both installers put the program in your own user folder and do not need admin rights.
But IT policy can still block downloads, scripts, or the companies’ websites. Typical signs: certificate or TLS errors, “running scripts is disabled”, or a 403 error.
Do not try to work around IT security. Send them the error message and the official install page.
Meanwhile, the desktop app may be available from your software centre.



Many of you work on laptops managed by the university. The installers themselves do not need administrator rights: they install into your own user folder. But managed machines can block things in other ways. Script execution may be disabled, the network may route through a proxy that breaks secure connections, or the download sites may be blocked. The error messages then mention certificates, TLS, a 403 code, or scripts being disabled. Please do not try to work around these restrictions yourself; they exist for good reasons, and bypassing them can violate university policy. Instead, send IT the exact error and the link to the official install page. In the meantime, the desktop app is often easier to get approved, and it may even be in your software centre already.

title: Accounts and installation
section: Where this goes wrong
text:
Where this goes wrong

Wrong plan. Signed in with a free Claude account: Claude Code will not work. Check which account the browser was logged into.
Wrong account. You have both a personal and an institutional login. The browser picks the one it remembers. Log out in the browser first if needed, then use /login in Claude Code or /logout and restart in Codex.
Old terminal window. The program is installed but “not found”. Open a new window.
Copied an outdated command from a blog or video. Use the exercise page.
Started in the wrong folder. The agent sees your home folder or Desktop. Exit, move to your empty folder, start again.
Region. Both services are available only in supported countries; an “unavailable in region” message is not something you can fix locally.


Let me collect the things that typically go wrong, so you recognise them. The first is the plan: someone signs in with a free Claude account and wonders why Claude Code will not work. The second is the account: many of us have a personal and a university login, and the browser quietly uses whichever it remembers. If the agent reports the wrong account, sign out in the browser and sign in again from the agent. The third is the old terminal window we discussed. The fourth is following an old blog post; these tools change fast, so stick to the exercise page. The fifth is starting the agent in the wrong folder. And finally, both services are only available in supported countries, which is rarely an issue here but good to know when travelling.
