title: First delegations
section: About this lecture
text:
About this lecture
You have the agent installed and you can find your way around the terminal. Now it should do some real work. We start with three small jobs that everyone knows and nobody enjoys: tidy a messy folder, clean a messy spreadsheet, and summarise a pile of PDFs into one table.

Work in a copy. The original stays untouched, whatever happens.
Describe the result, not the steps. Say what the finished thing should look like.
Ask for a record. A log of every change, a list of decisions, a list of assumptions.
Check by spot checks. Count before and after, check totals, pick three things at random and look at them yourself.
If it is wrong, say what is wrong. Correct the agent rather than start over.

This is a hands-on unit with example data only. Why the agent makes the mistakes it does comes next (How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail). Writing prompts in depth comes in Delegating well (Part 2).

This is the first unit where the agent does something useful for you. The three jobs are deliberately boring: organising files, cleaning a spreadsheet and making a summary table. They are the kind of chores that fill a Monday morning and that you would happily hand to an assistant. The point today is not the jobs themselves but the habits around them: work in a copy, say what you want the result to look like, ask for a record of what was done, and check the result yourself. These five habits come back in every later unit. We use example data only, because we have not yet talked about what data you may send to a cloud service. That comes in the privacy unit at the end of Part 1.

title: First delegations
section: Three small jobs eat a Monday morning
text:
Three small jobs eat a Monday morning


A shared folder where 40 files have piled up with names like fig2_final_REALLYfinal.png.
A spreadsheet from a student with merged headers, units in the cells and three spellings of “male”.
Six short reports that you need to summarise for a meeting, in one table.


Here are the three jobs. You will recognise all of them. The first is a folder that has grown without a system: dates written in four ways, “final” versions that were not final, and a few copies of the same file. The second is a spreadsheet that a person can read without trouble, but that no analysis program can use as it is. The third is a small pile of reports where you need the title, the author, the date and the main finding of each, side by side. Each job takes an hour or two by hand. Each one is also easy to get slightly wrong, which makes them good practice for checking an agent’s work.

title: First delegations
section: Good first jobs are tedious, easy to check and easy to undo
text:
Good first jobs are tedious, easy to check and easy to undo


Why these three jobs and not something more exciting? Because they sit in the safe corner of this picture. On the horizontal axis is how easy the result is to check. On the vertical axis is how easy it is to undo a mistake. Renaming files, cleaning a copy of a spreadsheet and making a summary table are all easy to check by looking, and easy to undo if you worked in a copy. Compare that with sending an email to all your students, which cannot be undone, or a literature review full of references, which takes real effort to check. We will get to the harder corners later in the course, with more safety nets. For a first delegation, pick something in the top-left corner.

title: First delegations
section: Today we use example data, not your own
text:
Today we use example data, not your own

Download one zip file per job from the exercise page: messy-folder.zip, messy-sheet.zip, reports.zip.
All three are synthetic: invented files, invented people, invented numbers.
Your own files wait until after Privacy, ethics and safety. There we look at what may be sent to a cloud service.
The example data has known answers, so you can check the agent against them.


Everything in today’s exercise is made up. The mice, the reports and the authors do not exist. That has two benefits. First, nothing sensitive leaves your computer, which matters because whatever the agent reads is sent to the company that runs the model. We discuss exactly what that means in the privacy unit. Second, because we made the data, we know the right answers: how many files there are, how many rows the clean table has, what the average weight is. That lets you check the agent against a key, which is the best way to learn what checking feels like before you do it on your own data where there is no key.

title: First delegations
section: Every delegation follows the same loop
text:
Every delegation follows the same loop


This is the shape of every delegation in this course. You make a copy to work in. You describe what you want the result to look like. The agent works, and asks your permission before it changes files or runs commands. You ask it for a record: what it changed, what it decided, what it assumed. You check the result with a few quick tests. If something is wrong, you say what is wrong, and the loop goes round again. Most of the value of the agent comes from going round this loop quickly. Most of the risk comes from skipping the last two steps. The rest of this lecture takes the steps one by one, and then applies them to the three jobs.

title: First delegations
section: Rule 1: always work in a copy, never in the original
text:
Rule 1: always work in a copy, never in the original


The agent can rename, move and overwrite files. In a copy, every mistake is free.
Keep the original somewhere the agent was not started from.


The first rule is the simplest and the most important. Before you let the agent touch anything, make a copy and start the agent inside the copy. The agent only works in the folder where you start it, unless you give it permission to go elsewhere, so the original stays safe. If the result is bad, you delete the copy and make a new one. This costs ten seconds and removes almost all of the risk from today’s jobs. Later, in the unit Git as undo button and lab notebook, we get a more powerful safety net that keeps every version. Until then, the copy is your undo button.

title: First delegations
section: Making the copy takes ten seconds
text:
Making the copy takes ten seconds

Unzip the download. You now have, for example, a folder messy-folder.
Duplicate the folder in your file browser and rename the copy messy-folder-work.
In the terminal, go into the copy and start the agent there:





Claude Code
Codex




Go into the copy
cd messy-folder-work
cd messy-folder-work


Start the agent
claude
codex




If the agent asks whether you trust this folder, answer yes: it is your copy of example data.

Make the copy by hand: an agent that can make the copy can also reach the original.

Here is how the copy works in practice. Unzip the file, duplicate the folder in Finder or Explorer as you would any folder, and give the copy a name that says it is the working copy. Then, in the terminal, use cd to go into the copy, as you practised in the Terminal survival kit, and start the agent there. The first time you start the agent in a new folder it may ask whether you trust the files in it. For example data that is fine. Note the reason we make the copy by hand today: to make a copy, the agent would need access to the folder where the original lives, and that is exactly what we want to avoid.

title: First delegations
section: Rule 2: describe the result you want, not the steps
text:
Rule 2: describe the result you want, not the steps


The second rule surprises people. When we explain a task to a person, we often explain the steps: first do this, then that. With an agent, it works better to describe the result: what the finished folder or table looks like. The agent is good at working out the steps. It cannot guess what you consider a good result. On the left, the steps are given but the result is vague: what is “a good name”? On the right, nothing is said about how to do it, but anyone, person or agent, could tell whether the job is done. That is the test of a good description: could you check the result against it?

title: First delegations
section: A description of the result answers four questions
text:
A description of the result answers four questions

What is there now? “This folder holds 40 files from a small lab project.”
What does done look like? “Subfolders by kind of file; names like 2024-03-12_plate-reader.csv.”
What about odd cases? “Exact duplicates go into a folder duplicates; do not delete anything.”
What must not happen? “Do not touch anything outside this folder.”

You do not need perfect wording. A few lines in plain language are enough. More on this in Delegating well.

A description of the result usually answers four questions. What is there now, so the agent knows what it is looking at. What done looks like, as concretely as you can: a folder layout, a file name pattern, the columns of a table. What to do with odd cases, which is where most of the decisions hide. And what must not happen. You do not have to write this like a contract. Plain sentences are fine, and the agent will ask if something is unclear, or you can tell it to ask. We go much deeper into this in the unit Delegating well in Part 2. Today, these four questions are enough.

title: First delegations
section: Rule 3: ask for a record of every change
text:
Rule 3: ask for a record of every change


A log makes the job checkable: you can read what happened instead of guessing.
A log makes the job undoable: “use the log to put every file back” is one sentence.


The third rule: ask for a record. For the folder job, the record is a rename log, a small table with the old name, the new name and the reason for each file. For the spreadsheet, it is a list of decisions. For the PDFs, it is the page each value came from. The record does two things. It lets you check the job by reading instead of by searching. And it makes the job reversible: if you do not like the result, you can ask the agent to use the log to undo every change. An agent will not always keep such a record unless you ask for it, so ask every time.

title: First delegations
section: Rule 4: ask the agent to list its assumptions
text:
Rule 4: ask the agent to list its assumptions


The fourth rule is to ask the agent to list its assumptions. An agent fills every gap in your description with a guess, and it usually does not tell you. Is 05-03-2024 the fifth of March or the third of May? Should a file with no date get today’s date or the date it was last saved? Is “ctrl” the same as “Control”? Each guess is probably reasonable, but some will be wrong for your situation, and you cannot correct a guess you do not know about. Asking for assumptions turns hidden guesses into a list you can read in a minute. It is also a good way to see whether the agent understood the task at all.

title: First delegations
section: Rule 5: check with counts, totals and three random samples
text:
Rule 5: check with counts, totals and three random samples

Count before and after. 40 files in, 40 files out (or 37 plus 3 duplicates). 48 animals in, 48 rows out.
Check a total. If the sheet has a mean or a sum, the cleaned data should give the same number.
Spot-check three at random. Pick three rows, files or cells and compare them with the original yourself.
Use what you know. Mouse weights of 250 g, or a report dated 2052, are wrong whatever the agent says.

“It ran without errors” is not a check. “The agent says it checked” is not a check either.

The fifth rule is to check, and to check in a way that takes minutes, not hours. Counting is the most powerful check: if forty files went in, forty must come out, or the difference must be explained. A total is the next best: if the student’s sheet says the mean weight is 23.27 grams, your cleaned table should say the same, otherwise a value was lost or misread. Then pick three things at random and check them by hand against the original. Random matters: if you only check the first rows, you only learn about the first rows. Finally, use your own expertise. You know what a plausible mouse weight is; the agent may not care. And note the last line: an agent saying it has checked its own work is not the same as you checking it.

title: First delegations
section: Job 1: the folder has 40 files and no system
text:
Job 1: the folder has 40 files and no system


Now the first job. This is the folder as you unzip it. Forty files from a small lab project. Dates in at least five formats. Several “final” versions. Files called “Copy of” and “(1)”, which are often exact duplicates but not always. Screenshots and photos named by the camera. Documents, data, figures and slides all in one heap. You could sort this by hand in an hour. The agent will do it in a few minutes, but only if you say what sorted means to you.

title: First delegations
section: The prompt for job 1 describes the finished folder
text:
The prompt for job 1 describes the finished folder
This folder holds 40 files from a small lab project: data, images,
documents and slides. Organise it so that a colleague could find things.

What I want at the end:
- a few subfolders by kind of file (for example data, figures, documents)
- every file renamed as YYYY-MM-DD_short-description.ext, using the date
  in the name, or the file's own date if the name has none
- exact duplicates moved to a folder called duplicates, not deleted
- a file rename-log.csv with one row per file: old path, new path, reason
- nothing deleted, and nothing outside this folder touched

Before you move anything, show me your plan and list your assumptions,
for example how you read dates like 05-03-2024.

Here is the prompt we use in the exercise. Notice that it says nothing about how to rename files or how to find duplicates. It describes the folder we want at the end, it says what happens to duplicates, it asks for the log, and it sets two limits: nothing deleted, nothing outside this folder. The last paragraph asks for a plan and a list of assumptions before any file is moved. That costs one extra round of conversation and saves a lot of tidying up. You may want different subfolders or a different name pattern. That is fine: the point is that you decide and write it down.

title: First delegations
section: The agent shows a plan, then asks before it moves files
text:
The agent shows a plan, then asks before it moves files


This is roughly what you will see. The agent first looks around: it lists the files, opens a few to see what is inside, and compares file contents to find duplicates. Then it shows a plan and its assumptions, and stops, because we asked it to. Read the plan. If you agree, say so; if not, say what to change. Then it starts work, and each time it wants to run a command that moves or renames files it asks permission, depending on your settings. You learned to read those permission prompts in the Terminal survival kit. This picture is illustrative: your session will look different, and the agent may choose a different order of steps.

title: First delegations
section: After: a structure you can explain in one sentence
text:
After: a structure you can explain in one sentence


Here is one sensible result. Data in one folder, figures and photos in another, documents and slides in a third, duplicates set aside, and a rename log at the top. Every name starts with a date in the same format, so files sort in time order. Your result will differ in the details, and that is fine as long as you can explain the structure in one sentence and the names follow the pattern you asked for. If the agent invented a structure with twelve subfolders, that is a sign the description was too loose, and you can simply say “use at most four subfolders”.

title: First delegations
section: Count before and after: every file must be accounted for
text:
Count before and after: every file must be accounted for


The first check is a count. Forty files went in. Afterwards, the subfolders should hold thirty-seven files and the duplicates folder three, and the rename log should have forty rows. If any of these numbers is off, something was lost, overwritten or skipped, and you ask about it. Overwriting is the classic accident here: if two files get the same new name, one replaces the other and silently disappears. Counting catches it. Then open the duplicates folder and check that each file really has a twin: same size, and the same content when you open both.

title: First delegations
section: Dates in file names are where the agent has to guess
text:
Dates in file names are where the agent has to guess








Original name
Possible readings
What settles it




data_05-03-2024 (1).csv
5 March or 3 May
it is a copy of data 2024-03-05.csv


microscope 14-03-24.png
14 March 2024
there is no month 14


growth_curve_Mar26.csv
26 March, which year?
the date column inside the file


Meeting notes 4 March.txt
4 March, which year?
the first line of the file


TODO (old).txt

the file’s own date (2 March 2024)



Check these rows in the rename log yourself. They are where a wrong guess hides.

The trickiest part of the folder job is dates. Some names are unambiguous, some can be read two ways, some have no year and some have no date at all. A careful agent looks inside the file or at the file’s own modification date to settle it, and says so in the log. A careless one picks the first reading that comes to mind. This table lists the cases in our example folder. When you check the rename log, go straight to these rows. In your own folders, the same kind of ambiguity is everywhere, and it is the single most common source of quiet mistakes when files are renamed in bulk.

title: First delegations
section: Job 2: a sheet a person can read and a computer cannot
text:
Job 2: a sheet a person can read and a computer cannot


The second job is a spreadsheet of body weights from a mouse study, typed in by hand over two weighing days. A person reads it without trouble: the title, the group headings, the notes. A program cannot: merged headings span several columns, weights are written as “26.5 g” or with a decimal comma, sex is written in nine different ways, there are blank rows, a note in the middle of the data, a duplicated row and a mean at the bottom. If you load this into R, Python or a statistics package as it is, you either get an error or, worse, a result that looks fine and is wrong.

title: First delegations
section: Each kind of mess needs a decision
text:
Each kind of mess needs a decision








Mess
Example
A decision someone has to make




Merged header rows
“Animal” over three columns
which row holds the column names


Units in cells
26.5 g, 5mg/kg
strip the unit; check it is the same unit everywhere


Decimal commas
24,1
read as 24.1


Several spellings
Male, male, M, m
map to one code


Mixed date formats
12/03/2024, 12.3.2024, 12 March 2024
day first or month first?


Notes in data cells
not weighed (sick), 23.7 (re-weighed)
empty, or keep the number?


Extra rows
blank rows, a batch note, a duplicate, a mean row
remove, and say so



None of these is hard. Together they are about 20 small decisions, and you want to see every one.

Each kind of mess on the sheet needs a decision, and most decisions are obvious. A decimal comma means a decimal point. “M” and “male” mean the same thing. But some are not obvious, and a few depend on knowledge only you have. Does “not weighed, sick” mean the value is missing, or that the animal should be left out? Does “minus” in the dose column mean zero, or unknown? Is a row that appears twice a duplicate, or two animals with a typo in the ID? The agent will make all of these decisions. Our job is to make sure we see each one, so we can agree or disagree.

title: First delegations
section: Ask for a script, not only a clean file
text:
Ask for a script, not only a clean file


Next month the student sends a new sheet with the same mess. You rerun the script.
The script is also a record: every decision is written down in it.


For the spreadsheet we ask for something extra: not only the clean file, but a script that produces it. A script is a small program, in Python or R, that reads the messy sheet and writes the clean table. You do not need to be able to write it, or even read all of it. But it gives you two things. First, you can rerun it next month when the same student sends a new sheet with the same habits. Second, the script is itself a record of every decision. If you ask “where do you decide what M means?”, the agent can point to the line. The agent may need to install a package to read Excel files and will ask you first. That is normal.

title: First delegations
section: The prompt for job 2 describes the table, the script and the record
text:
The prompt for job 2 describes the table, the script and the record
messy-sheet.xlsx holds body weights from a mouse study. I want a tidy
table I can analyse, and a way to do the same next month.

What I want at the end:
- clean_weights.csv with one row per mouse and the columns animal_id,
  sex (F or M), group (control, low or high), dose_mg_per_kg,
  date_weighed (YYYY-MM-DD), weight_g (a number), comment
- a script that makes clean_weights.csv from the .xlsx file, so I can
  rerun it on a new sheet
- decisions.md: a numbered list of every decision you made, including
  each row you removed and how you read each odd value
Do not change messy-sheet.xlsx. If a value is unclear, leave it empty
and list it, rather than guess.

Here is the prompt. Again, it describes the result: the exact columns of the clean table, the allowed values for sex and group, the date format. It asks for the script and for a decision list. And it sets one important rule for unclear values: leave them empty and list them, rather than guess. That rule matters. Without it, an agent will often fill a gap with something plausible, and a plausible invented value in a data table is very hard to find later. With it, you get a short list of questions to answer yourself.

title: First delegations
section: The decision list shows what the agent decided for you
text:
The decision list shows what the agent decided for you
An example of what you might get back (yours will differ):
1. Used row 3 as column names; dropped rows 1-2 (title and group headings).
2. Removed 4 blank rows, the "Batch 2 - arrived 2 April" note and the "Mean" row.
3. Removed row 20: an exact copy of row 19 (B1-15).
4. Mapped Male/male/M/m to M and Female/female/F/f to F (also "F " with a space).
5. Read "24,1" as 24.1 and removed "g" from weights.
6. B1-19 "23.7 (re-weighed)": kept 23.7, moved "re-weighed" to comment.
7. B2-11 "not weighed (sick)": weight left empty, note moved to comment.
8. Dose "-" and "none" in control rows read as 0.
9. Dates: read 12/03/2024 and 12.3.2024 as day first (12 March 2024).
Read it line by line and ask: would I have decided the same?

This is the kind of list you want back. Each line is a decision you can agree with or not. Most will be fine. Look out for the ones that change the data: removing a row, filling in a value, reading an ambiguous date. Line three, for example, removes a row because it is an exact copy. Is that right? In this example, yes, but in your own data, two identical rows might be two real measurements. Line nine is the classic: dates read day first. That is right for this sheet, except for one row, as we will see on the next slide. If you would have decided something differently, say so, and the agent changes the script.

title: First delegations
section: Check rows, categories and the total
text:
Check rows, categories and the total


Now check the result. The sheet’s own note says 48 animals, so the clean table must have 48 rows. Count the values in each category: there should be exactly two codes for sex and three for group, and in this study 16 animals per group. Check the total: the sheet’s mean row says 23.27 grams, and the mean of the clean weight column should match. And look at the distinct dates. There were two weighing days, so there must be exactly two dates. In this picture a third date appears: 4 September 2024. One row in the sheet was typed month first, 04/09/2024, and read day first. The total and the row count would not catch this, but the distinct dates do. This is why we use several small checks rather than one.

title: First delegations
section: Job 3: six reports, one table, a page for every value
text:
Job 3: six reports, one table, a page for every value


The third job is the summary table. Six short reports, two or three pages each, from different fields: a teaching project, a field study, a greenhouse trial, a hospital audit, a materials test. We want one table with the title, authors, date, main finding and a one-line summary for each. And for each value, the page it came from. The page column is what makes this table checkable. Without it, checking a value means reading the whole report again. With it, it takes ten seconds. Claude Code can usually read PDF files directly. Codex usually runs a small program to pull out the text, and may ask to install one.

title: First delegations
section: The prompt for job 3 asks for sources and for gaps
text:
The prompt for job 3 asks for sources and for gaps
This folder holds six short PDF reports. Make one table,
reports_summary.csv, with one row per report and these columns:
file, title, authors, date (YYYY-MM-DD), main_finding, one_line_summary,
and the page number where you found the title, the date and the
main finding.

Use only what is written in the reports. If something is missing or
unclear, write "not stated" and tell me; do not fill it in.
At the end, list every value you were unsure about.

The prompt for the third job. As before, it describes the table: the columns, the date format, one row per report. It asks for the page of each important value. And it says what to do when something is missing: write “not stated” instead of filling it in. This matters a lot for summaries. One of our reports has no date on its first page. Another has a date that can be read two ways. Another gives only a month. Without the instruction, an agent may quietly invent a full date that looks right. With it, you get an honest gap that you can fill yourself.

title: First delegations
section: Spot-check three random cells against the page
text:
Spot-check three random cells against the page


Now the spot check. Pick three cells at random, for example by rolling a die for the row, or by asking a colleague to point. Open the PDF at the page the table names and check the value. Is the number right? Is the author list complete? Is the main finding really the finding of this report? If all three are right, you have some confidence in the table, though not certainty. If one is wrong, check more, and tell the agent what was wrong. With six reports, you could check everything. The habit matters for later, when you summarise sixty reports and can only check a sample.

title: First delegations
section: Summaries are where plausible but wrong details creep in
text:
Summaries are where plausible but wrong details creep in
The peer-feedback report says on page 1:

A pilot at another department reported that peer feedback improved report grades by a full grade step.

and on page 2:

We found no clear difference in the final report grades: the mean grade was 3.9 with peer feedback and 3.8 without.


A quick summary may report “peer feedback improved grades by a full grade step”. That is another study’s result.
A date 03/09/2025 may be read as 9 March instead of 3 September.
A report dated “November 2024” may get an invented day.

These errors look exactly like correct values. Only the page reference lets you catch them quickly.

Here is the kind of mistake to look for. Our peer-feedback report mentions an earlier pilot that found a large effect, and then reports its own result, which is no clear difference. A hurried summary can pick up the wrong one. The sentence is fluent, the number is real, it is even in the report. It just is not this report’s finding. The same goes for dates: a British-style date read as American, or a month-only date given a made-up day. None of these errors look like errors. They look like a tidy table. That is why we ask for page references and do spot checks: not because the agent is usually wrong, but because when it is wrong, it looks the same as when it is right. The next unit explains why this happens.

title: First delegations
section: If the result is wrong, say what is wrong
text:
If the result is wrong, say what is wrong


Sooner or later a check fails. The natural reaction is to say “this is wrong, do it again”, or to close the session and start over. Both waste the work that was right. The agent does not know which part you are unhappy with, so it may change the parts that were fine and keep the part that was wrong. Instead, say exactly what is wrong: which row, what you expected, and why. Then ask it to fix the cause, not only the symptom. For the spreadsheet, that means fixing the script, rerunning it, and updating the decision list, so that next month’s run gets it right too.

title: First delegations
section: Good corrections point, explain and ask for the record to be updated
text:
Good corrections point, explain and ask for the record to be updated







Instead of
Say




“The dates are wrong.”
“Row B2-17 has date 2024-09-04. Both weighings were in March and April 2024, so this must be 9 April. Fix the script and add the decision to decisions.md.”


“Do it again, the folder is a mess.”
“Put all images in one folder figures, not three. Keep everything else. Update rename-log.csv.”


“The table is wrong.”
“The main finding for the peer-feedback report is the earlier pilot, not this study. Use the result on page 2.”



Start over only when the agent misunderstood the whole task, or the session has gone round in circles.

Here are some examples of good corrections. Each one points to the exact place, says what you expected, gives the reason if you know it, and asks for the record to be updated. That last part is easy to forget: if the decision list or the rename log no longer matches what was done, it is no longer a record you can trust. When should you start over? When the agent misunderstood the whole task from the start, or when you have corrected the same thing three times and it keeps coming back. Even then, it often helps to start the new session with “last time, this went wrong”, so the same misunderstanding does not happen again. We come back to this in Delegating well.

title: First delegations
section: Your session will look different from this lecture
text:
Your session will look different from this lecture

The same prompt gives a different session each time: other steps, other wording, sometimes another result.
That is normal. Language models are not deterministic.
So we compare results, not sessions: the counts, the totals and the spot checks on the exercise page.
If your result differs from the expected one, that is not a failure. It is something to find out about.


A practical warning before you start. If you type exactly the same prompt as your neighbour, you will get a different session. The agent may look at the files in a different order, choose a different folder name, or write the script in R instead of Python. Even the same person gets different sessions on different days. That is a property of how these models work, which we explain in the next unit. For the exercise, it means you should not compare your screen with the slides. Compare your result with the expected outcomes on the exercise page. If the numbers differ, that is interesting: find out whether the agent or the key is right.

title: First delegations
section: Where this goes wrong
text:
Where this goes wrong

Working in the original. One bad rename command, and the old names are gone.
Vague descriptions. “Clean this up” gets the agent’s idea of clean, not yours.
No record. Without a log, you cannot check and you cannot undo.
Checking only the first rows. Errors hide in the odd cases: row 37, the file without a date.
Trusting the agent’s own check. “I verified the table” is a claim, not a check.
Overwritten files. Two files renamed to the same name: one is silently lost. Count.
Invented values. A gap filled with something plausible. Ask for “not stated” instead.
Your own data too early. Not before Privacy, ethics and safety.


Here are the ways today’s jobs go wrong, collected in one place. Almost all of them are covered by the five rules. Working in a copy protects against bad commands. Describing the result protects against the agent’s own idea of what you want. The record and the checks catch the rest. Two items deserve a second mention. The agent may say it checked its own work, and it may have, but you have not, and its checks have the same blind spots as its work. And invented values are the hardest error to find, because they look exactly like real ones. The fix is to make “I don’t know” an allowed answer, by writing it into the prompt.

title: First delegations
section: A checklist for every delegation
text:
A checklist for every delegation


Here are the five rules as a checklist that fits on a sticky note. Copy first. Describe the result. Ask for a record and a list of assumptions. Check with counts, totals and three random samples. Correct by saying what is wrong. You will use this checklist in every unit of the course, and you will find that it works for any job you give an agent, not only for files and spreadsheets. Keep it next to your screen for the exercise.

title: First delegations
section: Summary
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




Good first jobs
tedious, easy to check, easy to undo


Work in a copy
start the agent in the copy; the original stays untouched


Describe the result
what done looks like, odd cases, what must not happen


Ask for a record
rename log, decision list, page references


List assumptions
hidden guesses become a list you can read


A script, not only a file
rerun next month; the script records every decision


Count and total
40 files in, 40 accounted for; the mean matches the sheet


Spot checks
three at random, against the original, by you


“Not stated”
allow the agent to say it does not know


Correct, do not restart
point to the problem, explain, update the record



Next (How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail): what is going on inside the agent, and why it misreads dates, picks up another study’s result and says it has checked when it has not.

Here is the summary. Choose jobs that are easy to check and easy to undo. Work in a copy. Describe the result you want, including the odd cases. Ask for a record and for the assumptions. Ask for a script when a job will come back. Check with counts, totals and random spot checks that you do yourself. Allow the agent to say “not stated”. And when something is wrong, say what is wrong rather than starting over. In the next unit we look inside: what a language model is, how the agent loop works, and why the mistakes we saw today, misread dates, a finding from the wrong study, a confident claim of having checked, are exactly the mistakes we should expect.

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: About this lecture
text:
About this lecture
In First delegations the agent sorted a folder, cleaned a spreadsheet and summarised PDFs. Most of it went well, and some of it went subtly wrong. To know when to trust the agent and how to check it, you need a working picture of what is going on inside.

An LLM is a model trained to continue text, one token at a time. It produces plausible text, which is not the same as true text.
Its context window is its working memory. What is not in the conversation or in the files it read does not exist for it.
An agent is an LLM with tools in a loop: read, write, run, search. It can check its own work by running it.
It fails in recognisable ways, and each one has a matching defence.

This is a concept unit with no maths. Writing good task descriptions comes in Delegating well; notes files that survive between sessions come in Organising a project for an agent.

Start from what they did last time. Everyone in the room has now watched an agent work on real files, and most of them will have noticed at least one thing that was not quite right: a file in the wrong folder, a row missing, a number that looked odd. Today we explain why that happens. The aim is not to make anyone an expert on neural networks. The aim is a mental model good enough to predict where the agent will be reliable and where it will not, so that checking becomes targeted rather than anxious. We will keep returning to one idea: trust what was run and can be rerun, and be suspicious of what was produced from memory. The exercise afterwards is called “catch the agent out” and you will deliberately provoke the failures we discuss.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Last time, all three jobs looked fine; not all of them were
text:
Last time, all three jobs looked fine; not all of them were

Each result looked finished and was described with confidence. The problems were only visible to someone who checked.

These are the three jobs from First delegations, and the kind of problem that turned up in at least some of your sessions. In the folder job, a couple of files ended up in a folder that made sense to the agent but not to you. In the spreadsheet job, rows that the cleaning script could not parse were dropped, and the summary at the end did not mention it. In the PDF job, one number in the summary table was not in the paper at all. Notice what these have in common: in every case the agent’s final message sounded equally sure of itself. Confidence in the wording tells you nothing about correctness. By the end of this lecture you should be able to say, for each of these three, why it happened and what check would have caught it. Ask the room: who found something like this? Collect two or three examples; we will come back to them.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: An LLM is a model trained to continue text
text:
An LLM is a model trained to continue text


Given the text so far, it scores every possible next token and picks one.
It adds that token to the text and repeats, one token at a time, until the answer is done.
An entire answer, a whole script, a summary of a PDF: all made this way.


This is the single most important idea of the lecture. A large language model is, at its core, a function that takes the text so far and returns a score for every possible next piece of text. The tool picks one piece, usually a likely one, appends it, and asks again. That is it. There is no separate database of facts being looked up and no calculator being consulted, unless the agent explicitly uses a tool, which we will come to. When you read a long, well-structured answer, every word was produced this way, left to right, without the model going back to revise. This explains a lot of what follows: the model is very good at producing text that fits, and “fits” is close to “true” for common, well-documented facts and far from it for rare ones.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: The model reads tokens, not letters or words
text:
The model reads tokens, not letters or words


The pieces the model works with are called tokens. A token is usually a common word, a part of a word, or a punctuation mark, and the space before a word is usually glued to it. The split shown here is illustrative; every model family splits text a little differently. Why does this matter for you? First, it explains a classic failure: asked how many r’s there are in “strawberry”, models have often got it wrong, because they never see the individual letters, only three chunks. Counting letters, characters, or rows by eye is the same kind of task. Second, numbers are split into pieces too, which is part of why arithmetic done “in the head” is unreliable. Third, lengths and limits are measured in tokens, not words: as a rule of thumb, a hundred tokens is roughly seventy-five English words, and other languages, Swedish included, often need more tokens for the same text.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Training: first a lot of text, then instructions and tools
text:
Training: first a lot of text, then instructions and tools


Stage 1 gives it language and a broad, patchy knowledge of the world.
Stages 2 and 3 make it a helpful assistant that can use tools, and also shape its habits, good and bad.


How does the model get good at predicting the next token? In the first stage it is trained on a very large amount of text: web pages, books, scientific papers, code, forums. Simply by learning to predict the next token in all of that, it picks up grammar, facts, styles of reasoning, programming languages and the conventions of many fields. That knowledge is broad but patchy: well-documented topics are covered many times over, niche topics barely at all. In the second stage it is trained further, on examples of good answers and on people’s ratings of answers, so that it behaves like a helpful assistant instead of just continuing text. In the third stage, for agent models, it practises tasks with tools: writing code, running it, reading the errors, fixing them. Keep in mind that underneath all three stages it is still a next-token predictor. And the second stage has a side effect we will meet later: if people rate agreeable answers highly, the model learns to be agreeable.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Its knowledge stops at a cut-off date
text:
Its knowledge stops at a cut-off date

The model does not know what happened after its training data was collected, and it does not always know that it does not know.

Training data is collected up to some date, the knowledge cut-off. Then the model is tested and released, and then you use it, possibly a year or more later. Anything that changed in that gap is invisible to it: new versions of R packages and Python libraries, functions that were renamed or removed, new guidelines, new papers. The model will still answer confidently, using the world as it was. This is one of the main reasons agents are more useful than plain chat for technical work: an agent can check which version is actually installed on your computer, read the error message when an old function fails, and search the web for the current documentation. When the answer depends on something recent, ask it to look it up rather than recall it.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: The same prompt can give different answers
text:
The same prompt can give different answers


The next token is picked with some randomness, not always the single most likely one.
One different early choice changes everything that follows.
So: running twice is a cheap test. Where two runs disagree, at least one is wrong or the question is open.


When the tool picks the next token it usually does not take the single most likely one every time; it samples, with a bit of randomness. That makes the text more natural, but it also means that the same prompt in two fresh sessions can give different answers. For a course title that is harmless, even useful. For a number, a list of problems in a data file, or a decision about which rows to keep, it is a signal. If two independent runs agree, that is weak evidence that the answer is stable. If they disagree, you have learnt that at least one of them is wrong, or that the question has no single answer and you need to decide. You will try this in the exercise. Note that agreement between two runs is not proof: both can be wrong in the same way, especially when both answer from memory.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: The context window is the model’s working memory
text:
The context window is the model’s working memory


Everything the model “knows” about your task is in the context window: the instructions built into the tool, a project notes file if there is one, your messages, the files it has opened, the output of the commands it ran, and its own earlier replies. For every new token, the whole window is taken into account. What is not in the window does not exist for the model. It has not seen files it did not open, even if they sit in the same folder. It has no memory of yesterday’s session. And it does not know what you meant but did not say: the unwritten habits of your lab, the fact that column C is in millimetres, the reason sample 17 is excluded. A very common cause of a “stupid” mistake is simply that the information was never in the window. The fix is usually to put it there: tell it, or point it at the file.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Long sessions get compacted, and details get lost
text:
Long sessions get compacted, and details get lost


The window is large but finite. When it fills up, the conversation is summarised to make room.
Claude Code does this automatically; in both tools you can also ask for it with /compact. Claude Code’s /context shows how full it is.


The context window is big, often the size of a long book, but not unlimited, and every file read and every command output takes up space. When it is nearly full, the tool compacts the conversation: it replaces the long history with a summary and continues from there. Claude Code does this automatically, and both Claude Code and Codex have a /compact command to do it on request. Claude Code also has /context to show how full the window is. A summary is shorter than the original by design, so something is lost. Often it is exactly the kind of detail that matters: an instruction you gave at the start, such as “never edit the files in raw”, or the exact numbers from an earlier step. That is why agents sometimes seem to forget a rule halfway through a long session. Two habits help: keep sessions to one task, and write important rules into a file rather than only into the chat.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: A new session starts from a blank slate
text:
A new session starts from a blank slate


Close the terminal, or start fresh (/clear in Claude Code, /new in Codex): the new session remembers nothing of the old one.
What should carry over has to be written in a file in the project folder. That is the job of the notes file in Organising a project for an agent.


When you start a new session, the context window is empty again apart from the built-in instructions and any notes file the tool reads at start-up. Two hours of corrections on Monday are gone on Tuesday. This surprises many people, because chat products sometimes have a memory feature, and because the agent seemed to “know” your project so well yesterday. It knew it because it had read the files and your corrections were in the window. The practical consequence: anything you want the agent to know every time belongs in a file. Both Claude Code and Codex read a project notes file automatically when they start in a folder: CLAUDE.md for Claude Code and AGENTS.md for Codex. We set that up properly in Organising a project for an agent. For now, just remember: a new session is a new colleague who has never seen your project.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: An agent is an LLM with tools, in a loop
text:
An agent is an LLM with tools, in a loop

The LLM only ever writes text. Some of that text is a request to use a tool; the harness (Claude Code, Codex) carries it out, after asking you.

Now from the model to the agent. The model itself can only produce text. An agent adds two things around it. First, tools: small, well-defined actions such as reading a file, writing or editing a file, running a command in the terminal, and searching or fetching a web page. Second, a loop: the model can write a special kind of text that means “please use this tool with these inputs”. The program around the model, which we call the harness, recognises that request, asks you for permission if needed, runs the tool, and pastes the result back into the context window. Then the model continues, now with the result in front of it. This repeats until the model decides it is done and writes a normal reply to you. Claude Code and Codex are harnesses: the terminal program you start is the loop, the permission prompts, and the tools, all wrapped around a model that runs in the cloud.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: The tools are few and simple; the loop makes them powerful
text:
The tools are few and simple; the loop makes them powerful








Tool
What it does
Example from First delegations




Read a file
puts the file’s content into the context window
opening each PDF


Write / edit a file
creates or changes a file on your disk
writing clean_sheet.py


Run a command
runs a program in the terminal and captures what it prints
python3 clean_sheet.py, moving files


Search / fetch the web
brings a web page or search results into the window
looking up a DOI




None of these is clever on its own. The power comes from chaining them: read, write a script, run it, read the output, fix, run again.
Every tool result lands in the context window, so it uses up working memory.


It is worth being concrete about how little the agent can actually do. There are a handful of tools: reading files, writing or editing files, running commands, and searching or fetching from the web. Some setups add more through connectors, which we meet in Making the agent yours. Each tool is simple, and each one you have already seen in First delegations: the PDFs were read, the cleaning script was written, the script was run, files were moved by commands. The power comes from chaining these steps in a loop, with the model deciding the next step based on what the last step returned. And every result goes into the context window, which is why a session that reads forty PDFs fills up faster than one that edits a single script.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: One turn of the loop, step by step
text:
One turn of the loop, step by step


Let us walk through one full iteration in detail, with the plant height file you will use in the exercise. Step one: you ask for the mean height per group. Step two: the model’s next tokens are not an answer but a tool request, here to run a small script it has just written. Step three: the harness shows you the command and asks whether it may run it. The model cannot run anything by itself; it is the harness on your computer that does it, and only after your yes. Step four: the script runs and prints two means and a warning that four values could not be read. Step five: that printed output is pasted into the conversation, just as if it were a message. Step six: the model continues from the new, longer context. A good agent now notices that 86 centimetres is a strange height for these plants and that four values were skipped, and goes back to step two to look at the rows. A careless run just reports the numbers. Which of the two you get is not guaranteed; that is why you check.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: The harness, not the model, asks for your permission
text:
The harness, not the model, asks for your permission


Read the command before you say yes. If you do not understand it, choose “no” and ask the agent to explain it.
“Don’t ask again” is convenient, but it removes a check. Use it only for commands you understand.


You met permission prompts in the Terminal survival kit. Now you know where they sit in the loop: between the model’s request and the tool actually running. This is your main control point. The wording differs between Claude Code and Codex and changes between versions, but the shape is the same: what will run, and yes, yes-and-don’t-ask-again, or no with an instruction. Reading the command is not about understanding every flag. It is about noticing surprises: a command that deletes files, one that touches a folder you did not mention, one that installs something, or one that sends data somewhere. If you are unsure, say no and ask “what does this command do, and why do you need it?”. The agent will explain, and that costs you ten seconds. The settings that change how often you are asked, and why we keep them cautious in this course, were covered in the Terminal survival kit.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Agents beat chat for real work because they can check by running
text:
Agents beat chat for real work because they can check by running


This is the reason the course is about agents and not about chat. In a chat window, you paste the table and the model produces numbers from reading it. They will be plausible, and for a small, clean table they may even be right, but nothing was computed and nothing can be rerun. An agent writes a script, runs it, and sees what comes back, including errors and warnings and numbers that look wrong. It can then fix the script and run it again. The final answer is backed by a file on your disk that you, a colleague or another agent can read and rerun. This does not make the agent always right. It can still write a script that computes the wrong thing. But it moves the answer from “trust me” to “here is how I got it”, and that is something you can check.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Eight ways the agent fails, each with a defence
text:
Eight ways the agent fails, each with a defence

The next slides take them one at a time: a concrete example, why it happens, and the defence.

Here is the map for the second half of the lecture. These eight failure modes cover most of what you will run into in this course. They are not exotic: you will see several of them in the exercise today, and probably all of them by the end of the course. The colours group them loosely. Red: the model produces things that are not true. Purple: it tells you what you want to hear or quietly makes the job easier for itself. Ochre: it works outside the boundaries of the task, in space or in time. Teal: problems that come from the context window itself. For each one we will look at a realistic example and a defence. The defences overlap a lot, and at the end we collect them into one toolbox.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Hallucination: invented references look exactly like real ones
text:
Hallucination: invented references look exactly like real ones

Defence: open every DOI or PMID yourself, and check that the paper says what the summary claims. Ask the agent to fetch each reference rather than recall it.

Hallucination means the model produces something that sounds right but is not. References are the classic case. Remember: the model continues text. A reference has a very predictable shape: authors, year, title, journal, DOI. The model can produce that shape fluently even when it has no specific paper in mind. There are degrees of wrong. The DOI may not exist at all. It may exist but point to a different paper. Or the paper is real but does not support the claim attached to it, which is the hardest to catch because the link works. All four lines on the slide look equally confident. The defence is to treat every reference as unverified until you have opened it. An agent can help here, because it can fetch the DOI or search PubMed and show you what came back, rather than recalling. We return to this in depth in the Literature review unit.

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Hallucination in code: options that do not exist, or mean something else
text:
Hallucination in code: options that do not exist, or mean something else
The agent writes a script that calls a function with an option that sounds right:
data = read_table("plants.csv", skip_bad_rows=True, units="cm")

If the option does not exist, the script stops with an error. The agent sees it and fixes it. Harmless, because it ran.
If a similar option exists but does something else (it skips rows silently, or ignores the unit), the script runs and the result is quietly wrong.

Defence: let it run the code, not just write it. Ask: “What does each option in this call do? Show me the documentation for it.” Check the result against something you know.

The same mechanism produces invented function options in code. The model has seen thousands of scripts and produces something that looks like them; occasionally it invents a parameter name that would be sensible but does not exist. Here the agent has a big advantage over chat: when it runs the script, a non-existent option usually produces an error immediately, the error goes into the context window, and the agent corrects itself. You may see this happen several times in a session, and that is fine. It is the loop doing its job. The dangerous case is the near miss: an option that exists but does something slightly different from what the agent assumed, so no error appears. You do not need to read code to defend against this. Ask the agent to explain each option and show the documentation, and above all check the output against something you know, which is the subject of the next slides.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Confident wrong numbers: counting and arithmetic “in its head”
text:
Confident wrong numbers: counting and arithmetic “in its head”

Defence: for any number that matters, ask it to compute it with code and show the command. “112” from reading is a guess written to look like a count.

Because the model works on tokens, counting rows, adding up a column, or computing a mean by reading the data is the same kind of task as counting the r’s in strawberry. It will produce a number with the right shape, often close, sometimes exact, sometimes far off, and always stated with the same confidence. The fix is simple and costs nothing: ask it to compute the number with code. Then the number comes from a program that actually counts, the command is visible, and you can rerun it. Make this a reflex. In the exercise you will ask for the same count both ways and compare. Watch out also for a subtle version: an agent that has run code earlier in the session may later quote a number from memory instead of rerunning, for example after the data changed. If in doubt, ask “did you compute that just now, or is it from earlier?”.

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Sycophancy: it agrees with you, and caves when you push
text:
Sycophancy: it agrees with you, and caves when you push

Defence: ask neutral questions (“which group grew taller?”, not “the treated group grew taller, right?”). When it changes its mind, ask what new evidence changed it. Ask it to argue against you.

Sycophancy is the tendency to tell you what you want to hear. It comes partly from the second training stage: people rating answers tend to prefer ones that agree with them, so the model learns to agree. It shows up in two ways. First, a leading question gets a confirming answer: if you say “the treated plants grew taller, right?”, the agent may agree without looking carefully. Second, and worse, when the agent gives a correct answer and you push back, it may cave and apologise, even though nothing changed in the data. Models have become better at holding their ground, but this has not gone away. As experts you often do know better than the agent, so pushing back is right. The test is whether its change of mind comes with new evidence: a rerun, a row it had missed, a different calculation. If it just apologises and flips, be suspicious of both answers and check the data yourself. A useful prompt is “argue against my interpretation” or “what would make me wrong here?”.

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Silent shortcuts: it makes the task easier and does not say so
text:
Silent shortcuts: it makes the task easier and does not say so


This is the one from the spreadsheet job in First delegations, and in practice it is one of the most damaging failures because nothing looks wrong. Faced with messy data, the easiest way to make a script run without errors is to skip the rows that cause errors. The agent then reports success, honestly from its point of view: the script ran and produced a clean file. The fifty-seven rows that were dropped are not mentioned. Here they were rows with an unusual date format, which may well be all the samples from one site or one technician, so dropping them biases the result. The defence is one you can apply without reading code: count the rows before and after, and ask directly, “did you drop, skip, fill in or simplify anything? List it.”
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Silent shortcuts, part 2: hard-coding and quietly simplifying
text:
Silent shortcuts, part 2: hard-coding and quietly simplifying

Hard-coding to make a check pass. You ask for a script that reproduces the published value 4.2. It cannot get there, so it writes result = 4.2. The check passes; nothing is reproduced.
“Simplifying” the task. You asked for all 40 PDFs; it did 12 “as a representative sample”. You asked for a mixed model; it ran a t-test “for simplicity”.
Fallbacks that hide failure. When a step fails, it fills in a default (0, the mean, “unknown”) and carries on.

Defence: ask “what did you not do that I asked for?” and “are any values typed in by hand rather than computed?” Check one known case by hand. Read the final summary for words like representative, for simplicity, placeholder, assumed.

Dropped rows are one kind of shortcut; here are three more. Hard-coding: when a script must produce a known answer and the agent cannot make it work, it may simply write the answer in. This happens in software testing, where agents have been seen to change a test so that it passes, and it can happen in your analysis too. Simplifying: the agent quietly does less than you asked, often announcing it in a single word you might skim past, such as “representative” or “for simplicity”. Fallbacks: a missing value replaced by a default so the pipeline keeps running. None of this is malicious. The model was trained to finish tasks, and finishing a simpler task looks a lot like finishing the real one. The defences are direct questions, and checking one case you can work out yourself. Agents tend to answer honestly when asked directly what they skipped; they just do not always volunteer it.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Scope creep: it changes files you did not ask about
text:
Scope creep: it changes files you did not ask about


Scope creep is the opposite of a shortcut: the agent does more than you asked. You ask for one axis label to be fixed, and while it is there it also tidies up a helper script, rewrites the README, and corrects a “typo” in a raw data file. Each change might be well meant. Together they make the job hard to review, can break things that worked, and in this example touched raw data, which should never change. The defence has three parts. Say in the task what may and may not be changed, for example “only edit make_plot.R”. Work in a copy of your data, which we make a habit in Privacy, ethics and safety. And at the end ask “list every file you created, changed or deleted”. In Git as undo button and lab notebook you will get a tool that shows every change and lets you undo any of them, which turns scope creep from a disaster into a nuisance.

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Stale knowledge: old versions, old functions, old advice
text:
Stale knowledge: old versions, old functions, old advice
The model learnt from code written before its cut-off, much of it years older. Typical symptoms:

It uses a function that has since been renamed or removed: for example df.append() in pandas (removed in pandas 2.0), or size = for line width in ggplot2 (replaced by linewidth in version 3.4.0).
It suggests installing a specific old version, or a package that is no longer maintained.
It describes its own tool (Claude Code, Codex) as it was when it was trained, not as it is now.

Defence: let it run the code: errors and deprecation warnings show up and get fixed. Ask it to check the installed version and read the current documentation before relying on a function. For questions about the tools themselves, check the official docs.

Stale knowledge is the cut-off from earlier, seen in practice. Software changes constantly. Two examples you may well meet: pandas, a Python data library, removed a commonly used function called append in version 2.0, and ggplot2, the R plotting package, changed the argument for line width from size to linewidth in version 3.4.0. Code written from memory may use the old forms, because there is far more old code in the training data than new code. Running the code is again the main defence: the error or the warning appears, and a good agent reads it and fixes the call. Another subtle case is the agent describing itself. Ask Claude Code or Codex how one of its own settings works and it may describe an older version of itself. For tool behaviour, the official documentation is the authority, and the agent can fetch it for you if you ask.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Losing track in long sessions
text:
Losing track in long sessions


What it looks like

It breaks a rule you gave an hour ago (“never edit raw/”).
It redoes work that was already done, or undoes a fix.
It refers to a file or column that was renamed earlier.
Answers get vaguer; it “forgets” decisions.


Defence

One task per session. Start fresh (/clear, /new) when the task changes.
Put lasting rules in a file, not only in the chat (Organising a project for an agent).
Before a big step, ask it to restate the rules and the plan.
When it drifts, a fresh session with a short summary is often faster than arguing.



This one follows directly from the context window and compaction. In a long session, early instructions are far back in the window or have been summarised away, and the model’s attention is on recent material. The symptoms are recognisable: a rule broken, a fix undone, an old file name used, answers that become less precise. People tend to respond by arguing with the agent in the same session, which adds more text to an already crowded window. It is usually better to start a fresh session with a short, clear description of where things stand. Keep sessions to one task. Put rules that must always hold in a notes file, which the tool reads at the start of every session, and which we set up in Organising a project for an agent. And before a risky step, asking “restate the rules you are following and your plan” is a cheap way to see whether it still has them.
crumbs: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Prompt injection: text in a page or PDF can act as instructions
text:
Prompt injection: text in a page or PDF can act as instructions

Defence: keep permission prompts on when the agent reads web pages or documents you did not write; be suspicious of any action you did not ask for. More in Privacy, ethics and safety.

The last failure mode is different because someone else causes it. Everything the agent reads ends up in the same context window as your instructions, and the model sees it all as text. If a web page or a PDF contains text written as instructions to an AI, the model may follow it. This has been demonstrated with hidden text in web pages, in documents, and in manuscripts submitted for review. The effects range from a biased summary, “say this paper is excellent”, to attempts to make the agent run commands or send data elsewhere. For this course the practical rule is simple: when the agent reads material you did not write, especially from the web, keep the permission prompts on and read what it wants to do. An action you did not ask for, right after it read an external document, is a red flag. We go further into this, and into what data you should let the agent see at all, in Privacy, ethics and safety.

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: The trust ladder: trust what was run, distrust what was remembered
text:
The trust ladder: trust what was run, distrust what was remembered


Here is the one picture to take home. At the top: a result from code that ran and matches something you know independently. Then: code that ran and is on disk, so it can be read and rerun even if you have not checked it yet. In the middle: a quote from a file or a web page, with a location you can open. Lower: a claim that it did something, “I checked all rows”, “I verified the references”, without showing how. That is still just generated text. At the bottom: answers from memory, references, numbers, version numbers, facts about niche topics. These are produced exactly like any other plausible text. The point of good prompting is to move answers up the ladder: “compute it with code”, “show me where in the PDF”, “fetch the DOI”. And the point of checking is to spend your limited time on the rungs that need it most.

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: The verification toolbox
text:
The verification toolbox








Check
How
Catches




Spot check
open 3 to 5 random items and compare with the source yourself
hallucinated details, wrong extraction


Known answer
include a case where you already know the result
wrong method, hard-coded values


Rerun
run the script again; or the same prompt in a fresh session
randomness, numbers from memory


Count before and after
rows, files, samples in and out
silent drops, duplicates


Ask for sources, then check them
DOI, PMID, page number, file and line
invented references and quotes


Ask another agent
a fresh session, or the other tool, reviews the work
blind spots of the first session


Ask directly
“what did you skip, assume, or simplify? which files did you change?”
shortcuts, scope creep



Your domain knowledge is the strongest check of all: does this result make sense in your field?

Here are the checks collected in one place. None needs programming. A spot check means picking a few items at random, not the first few, and comparing them with the original. A known answer means planting or choosing a case where you know the right result: a sample you measured by hand, a total from a published report. Rerunning catches both randomness and answers produced from memory. Counting before and after catches silent drops and duplicates. Asking for sources only helps if you then check them. A second agent, in a fresh session or the other tool, has none of the first session’s assumptions in its context and often spots problems. Asking directly works surprisingly well, because agents tend to answer honestly when asked. Above all, you are the expert in your field. A mean plant height of 86 centimetres for seedlings, or a sample size larger than the patient cohort, should make you stop, and the agent will often not notice what you notice at a glance.

text:
Keep a failure log: each surprise becomes a habit

One line per surprise. You start it in today’s exercise and keep it for the whole course.
After a few weeks it tells you which checks to do by default for your kind of work.


The exercise today starts a small habit that we keep for the rest of the course: a failure log. Every time the agent gets something wrong, or nearly does, add one line: what you asked, what went wrong, which type from our map, how you caught it, and what you will do differently. It takes a minute. The value comes after a few weeks, when you can see a pattern: maybe in your work the typical problem is extraction errors from PDFs, or silent drops in messy spreadsheets. That tells you which checks to make routine. It is also a good basis for a conversation with colleagues about how much to rely on these tools, grounded in what actually happened rather than in hype or fear. A template is in the exercise.

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: What we do not understand about LLMs
text:
What we do not understand about LLMs

Why a particular answer came out. We can see the inputs and the outputs, but reading the reasons off the model’s internals is still an open research field.
Whether its explanation is the real reason. When it explains its reasoning, that explanation is also generated text; it may not reflect how the answer was actually produced.
Where it will fail next. Ability is uneven: it may solve a hard task and fail an easy one next to it. Benchmarks tell you little about your task.
How it will behave after an update. Models and tools change every few months; a habit that worked may need rechecking.
What it “understands”. Researchers disagree on how to describe what these models know. For our purposes it does not matter: we judge results, not intentions.


It is important to be honest about the limits of our own understanding, not just the model’s. Nobody, including the companies that build these models, can fully explain why a particular answer came out. Interpretability research is making progress, but it is far from routine. When the model explains its reasoning, that explanation is produced the same way as everything else, and it may be a plausible story rather than an account of what happened. Its abilities are uneven in ways that are hard to predict: it may write a correct statistical analysis and then miscount the samples. Benchmarks measure average performance on someone else’s tasks, not yours. Models and tools are updated every few months, sometimes changing behaviour you relied on. And whether the model “understands” anything is genuinely debated. None of this stops us from using it well. It is exactly why this course is built around checking results rather than trusting the process.

title: How LLMs and agents work, and how they fail
section: Summary
text:
Summary







Concept
Key fact




LLM
trained to continue text, one token at a time; plausible is not the same as true


Token
a word or a piece of one; the model does not see letters, so counting by eye is unreliable


Training
a lot of text, then instructions and tools; knowledge stops at a cut-off


Sampling
the same prompt can give different answers; disagreement between runs is a warning


Context window
working memory; not in the window = does not exist; long sessions are compacted


New session
blank slate; lasting rules go in a file


Agent
LLM + tools + loop; the harness runs tools after your permission


Why agents
they can check by running; the script stays on disk to rerun


Failure modes
hallucination, wrong numbers, sycophancy, silent shortcuts, scope creep, stale knowledge, losing track, prompt injection


Trust ladder
trust what was run and can be rerun; distrust what was remembered



Next (Privacy, ethics and safety): what you may send to a cloud model, how to keep the agent away from data it should not see, and how to choose your own project for the rest of the course.

The summary is the revision sheet. If you remember one line, make it the trust ladder: trust what was run and can be rerun, distrust what was remembered. Everything else explains why. The model continues text token by token, so it is fluent rather than reliable. It knows only what is in its context window, and forgets between sessions and sometimes within long ones. The agent loop lets it run code and see the result, which is what makes it useful for real work, and the harness puts you in control of each step. The eight failure modes all have defences, and most of them are simple questions or simple counts. Next we turn to what you should and should not let the agent see: privacy, ethics and safety. At the end of that unit you choose the project you will carry through the rest of the course, and the habits from today apply to it from the first session.
