title: Exercise: privacy, ethics and safety, and choosing your own project
section: Worked example
text:
Worked example

Part 1: Classify six scenarios
No agent needed. For each scenario, decide: allowed, allowed with precautions (say which), or not allowed. Use the flowchart and write one sentence of reasoning. Assume a personal Claude Pro or ChatGPT Plus account with training turned off, and a university that has not approved that account for personal data.
A. Grade distribution. A teacher has the learning platform’s export of last year’s exam: student names, personal identity numbers, emails, points per question, and a note column (“extra time”, “ill”). They want plots of the points per question and a short report.
B. Open-access literature table. A researcher has downloaded 15 open-access papers under CC BY from PubMed Central and wants a table with organism, sample size and main finding for each.
C. Reviewing a proposal. A researcher has been asked to review a grant proposal for the Swedish Research Council. They want the agent to summarise the proposal’s methods section to save time.
D. Survival analysis. A clinical researcher wants an R script for a survival analysis on an export of patient records from the hospital’s system (diagnosis codes, dates, age, sex). The study has ethics approval.
E. Industrial test data. An engineer has a folder of fatigue-test measurements on steel samples, made in a project with a company. The collaboration agreement says results are confidential until both parties approve publication. No people are involved.
F. Next month’s exam. A teacher wants the agent to draft ten new exam questions for next month’s exam, using last year’s exam (already published on the course page) as a model.






Answers and reasons





A. Not allowed as it stands; allowed with precautions in another form. The file holds personal data (names, IDs, emails), and the note column holds health data (“ill”, “extra time” for a disability), which is a special category. A personal plan is not approved for it. The safe route is the one from the lecture: describe the columns, let the agent build and test the script on a synthetic stand-in, then run the script on the real file yourself with the agent closed. Removing the identifying columns yourself (in Excel, before the agent sees the file) and dropping the note column would also help, but the remaining data is still personal data if a student can be identified, so check with your university.
B. Allowed. Public, openly licensed material. Respect the licence (CC BY requires attribution, which the table should keep), and check the extracted numbers against the papers: the agent can misread tables.
C. Not allowed, never. The proposal was given in confidence. The Swedish Research Council does not allow generative AI in the scientific assessment, and uploading any part of a proposal to an AI service breaks the confidentiality promise. This holds even for one section, and even with training off.
D. Not allowed for the data; allowed with precautions for the script. Patient data is sensitive personal data, and the ethics approval almost certainly specifies where the data may be processed; a cloud AI tool is not on that list. The agent may write the script on a synthetic dataset with the same columns and realistic value ranges; the researcher then runs it in the approved secure environment, without the agent. Check with the study’s data controller before you even describe rare features of the cohort.
E. Allowed with precautions, depending on the contract. There is no personal data, but the results are confidential under an agreement. Read the clause on third parties; if it forbids processing by third-party services, an AI provider counts, and the answer is not allowed. If it is silent, ask the partner. An institutional plan with a data processing agreement is a much better basis than a personal one.
F. Allowed with precautions. Last year’s exam is public, so using it as a model is fine. The new questions are confidential until the exam: keep training off (or use an institutional plan), keep the folder private, and do not push it to a public GitHub repository (Part 3). And check every question and answer yourself: you are responsible for the exam.





Part 2: Find your university’s AI policy
Here the agent searches the web for you. Nothing private is involved: the prompt contains only your university’s name.

Open a terminal and go to your course folder (cd, as in Terminal survival kit). Start the agent there (claude or codex). If Codex says the folder is not under version control and suggests read-only, accept that: this part needs no file edits.
Type this prompt, with your university’s name filled in:

Search the web for <my university>'s official policy or guidelines on
using generative AI tools (like ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot) for staff:
teachers and researchers. I want:
1. the link to the official policy page (on the university's own website),
2. which AI tools the university has approved, and for which kinds of
   data (public, internal, personal, sensitive),
3. any rules on AI use in teaching, exams and theses,
4. who to contact with questions (data protection officer, IT, library).
Only use pages on the university's own domain or its official intranet.
For every claim, give the exact link where you found it. If you cannot
find something, say so instead of guessing.
Do not create or change any files.

When the agent asks to search or fetch a web page, read the request and approve it. If it proposes anything else, such as writing a file, say no.
Copy the answer somewhere you can find it (you will use it in the README below).







Tip



If your university’s policy is behind a login (an intranet), the agent cannot read it. Then it will find at most a public summary. Open the intranet yourself and look for “AI”, “generative AI” or “ChatGPT” in its search.




Check the result

Open every link the agent gave you. Is it on your university’s own domain? Does the page actually say what the agent claimed? Agents sometimes produce plausible links that do not exist, or summarise a page wrongly (How LLMs and agents work).
Look for the date on the policy page. Policies from 2023 and 2024 are often replaced; make sure you have the current one.
Find the approved tools list yourself if the agent did not. If it does not exist, write down who to ask.
Check your account setting from the table in Before you start by opening the settings page, not by asking the agent.
Compare your Part 1 answers with the solutions. Where you differed, was it because your own university’s policy says something different? That is a good thing to notice.

title: Exercise: privacy, ethics and safety, and choosing your own project
section: On your own project
text:
On your own project
Now choose the project you will keep for the rest of the course. Every exercise from Delegating well on has an “On your own project” part that applies to it.






Warning



Privacy reminder. Do not give the agent any of your project’s data in this exercise. You only describe the project, in your own words, and that description goes to the provider. Do not put names of students, patients, colleagues, or confidential details into the description.



Step 1: Choose a project
A good project is:

Real: something your job needs, not a toy.
Small: a first useful result within a few sessions. You can grow it later.
Yours: from your own field, so you can tell a right answer from a wrong one.
Safe: data you may give to the agent, or a plan for a synthetic stand-in.
Checkable: you can already say how you would verify the result.

You can swap projects later. If you have no idea yet, pick one from the list below.


Example projects
Each example says what you would build, where the data comes from, and how you would check it. All of them are privacy-safe as described.

For teachers
A course page with one interactive demo. Take one of your own courses and build a small website with the course description, schedule and one interactive page that explains a hard concept (for example how a sample mean varies with sample size, how a lens forms an image, or how compound interest grows). Data: your own public course material. Good result: a page a student can use without you explaining it. Check: let a colleague or a student try the demo and explain back what it shows; compare the demo’s numbers with a hand calculation. (Builds on A course or project page and Interactive demos.)
A question bank with variants and answer keys. Turn a set of your own published exercises into a structured bank (one file per question, with topic and difficulty), and let the agent generate numeric variants with answer keys. Data: your own exercises (keep unreleased exam questions private). Good result: 20 questions, each with three variants and a correct key. Check: solve a random sample of variants yourself; the agent’s keys must match.
Course evaluation numbers as a short report. Turn the numeric part of last year’s course evaluation (the averages and counts per question, as published to students or the programme board) into a report with plots and a comparison with earlier years. Data: aggregated numbers only; leave out free-text comments, which often identify people. Good result: a two-page report you could hand to the programme board. Check: recompute two averages by hand from the source table.


For researchers in biology and medicine
A literature map of 20 genes or proteins. Choose 20 genes, proteins or pathways from your field. Build a table with, for each, its function, three key papers with verified PMIDs or DOIs, and the organisms studied. Data: PubMed and open-access papers. Good result: a table you would trust in a review article draft. Check: look up every reference in PubMed; open five papers and confirm the claimed finding. (Builds on Literature review.)
Reanalysis of a public dataset. Pick a published RNA-seq dataset from GEO or an image set from the Broad Bioimage Benchmark Collection, and reproduce one figure from the paper. Data: public, with a licence or terms you check first. Good result: your figure next to the published one. Check: the main result matches the paper (direction, rough size); differences are explained. (Tracks A and C.)
A Shiny app for your lab’s measurement data. An app where lab members can filter and plot non-personal measurements, such as plate-reader runs, growth curves or instrument QC values. Data: lab data with no people in it; copies only. Good result: a colleague can answer a real question with the app in two minutes. Check: reproduce one plot from the app by hand in Excel. (Builds on Shiny apps.)


For researchers in engineering and natural sciences
An automated weekly report from instrument logs. Instruments, sensors and simulations write log files. Build a script that reads a week of logs and produces a one-page summary: uptime, ranges, warnings, a plot. Data: log files with no personal data (check that user names are not in them). Good result: a report you would actually read every Monday. Check: count warnings in one log file by hand and compare.
Making an old analysis reproducible. Take an analysis that only works on one computer (an old MATLAB, R or Python script, or an Excel workbook) and turn it into one script with pinned package versions and a README that lets a new student rerun it. Data: your own analysis and its input data (copies). Good result: someone else reruns it and gets the same numbers. Check: the new script’s output equals the old output to the last reported digit. (Builds on Reproducible figures and Reading other people’s code.)
A table of material properties from papers. Collect one property (for example the thermal conductivity, Young’s modulus or band gap of a class of materials) from 20 to 30 open-access papers into one spreadsheet with a “source page” column. Data: open-access PDFs. Good result: a table you would cite. Check: verify a random sample of five values against the papers by hand. (Builds on Extracting data from PDFs.)


For researchers in the humanities and social sciences
The funding landscape of your field. Who funds research like yours in Sweden or the EU, how much, and how has it changed? Use Swecris (Swedish funders, with an API) or CORDIS (EU projects, open data). Data: public grant records. Good result: three plots and a paragraph you could put in your next application’s background. Check: compare yearly totals with the funder’s own published statistics. (Builds on Collecting and analysing grant results.)
A cleaned, documented open dataset ready for deposit. Take a dataset you have built (a corpus of public-domain texts, a coded table of historical records with no living persons, a set of public documents) and make it deposit-ready for Zenodo: tidy files, a data dictionary, a README, a licence. Data: your own, non-personal or already-public material. Good result: a colleague understands each column from the documentation alone. Check: a colleague answers three questions about the data using only the README.
Preparing your next grant application. Collect the published panel members for a call you plan to apply to, build an expertise profile for each from public sources (ORCID, OpenAlex), and have the agent write mock reviews of your own draft from several perspectives, using the funder’s criteria. Data: public information about people (still personal data: keep it for your own preparation) and your own draft. Good result: a list of weak points to fix before submission. Check: compare each profile with the person’s own web page; judge whether the mock reviews raise points a real reviewer would. (Builds on Likely reviewers. Never contact or lobby reviewers.)



Step 2: Fill in the worksheet
Answer these in a text editor (or on paper) in a few sentences each. Keep personal and confidential details out.

Project title. A short name, and a folder name without spaces (for example soil-funding-map or course-page-cellbio).
Goal. What will exist at the end that does not exist now?
Who could use it? You, your students, your group, a programme board, reviewers?
What data? What files, from where, roughly how large? Who owns them, and under what licence or agreement?
Data class. Public, internal, personal, sensitive personal or confidential? Run the data through the flowchart and write the outcome.
Precautions. Which ones follow from the data class (training off, synthetic stand-in, approved tool, keep the folder private)? What must never go into the folder?
What a good result looks like. Be concrete: “a plot of X against Y for all 12 sites”, not “nice figures”.
How you will check it. A known answer, a hand calculation, a sample checked against the source, a colleague’s review.
Your university’s rules. The link to your AI policy from Part 2, and the contact person.

If your data class is sensitive or your data is given in confidence, choose a different project, or plan from the start to work only on a synthetic stand-in. If you are unsure, ask your data protection officer before the next unit.


Step 3: Create the project folder
The agent creates the folder and writes your answers into a README.md. That is all the folder holds for now; it gets its proper structure in Organising a project for an agent.

Start the agent in your course folder (the parent of the new project folder), not in your home folder.
Make sure the agent may create files. In Claude Code, the status line shows the mode; manual mode is fine, you will approve each step. In Codex, if the session is read-only, type /permissions and choose the mode that lets Codex edit files in the folder (not full access).
Type this prompt, with your own answers pasted at the end:

Create a new folder called <folder-name> inside the current folder.
In it, create only one file, README.md, with these sections:

# <Project title>
## Goal
## Who could use it
## Data
## Data class and precautions
## What a good result looks like
## How I will check it
## University AI policy
## Log of AI use

Fill the sections from my worksheet answers below. Keep my wording;
fix only spelling. Under "Data class and precautions", add a short
list called "Never put in this folder" based on my answers.
Under "Log of AI use", add one line: today's date, the tool and plan I
use, and "created this README from my worksheet".
Do not create any other files or folders. Show me the README when done.

My worksheet answers:
<paste your answers here>

Read each action before you approve it. The agent should ask to create one folder and one file, nothing else.










Claude Code
Codex




Start in the course folder
claude
codex


If it cannot write files
Press Shift+Tab until the status line shows a mode that allows edits, or approve each edit when asked
/permissions, choose the mode that allows edits in the workspace


Show the README afterwards
Ask: “show me README.md”
Ask: “show me README.md”





Check the result

Open the new folder in your file browser. It contains exactly one file, README.md. No data, no copies, no other files.
Open README.md in a text editor. Every section is there, the wording is yours, and the agent has not added claims you did not make (for example a promise about data you do not have, or a different goal).
The “Never put in this folder” list matches what the flowchart said for your data.
The policy link opens and is the page you checked in Part 2.
Nothing in the README is personal or confidential: you could show it to a colleague from another university without worry.

section: Before you start
text:
Before you start

You have installed Claude Code and/or Codex and signed in (Accounts and installation). If claude or codex gives “command not found”, go back to that unit first.

title: Exercise: find your way around
section: Worked example
text:
Worked example

Step 1: Open a terminal

macOSWindowsLinux


Press Cmd+Space, type Terminal and press Enter. A window opens with a line ending in % (or $).


Press the Windows key, type PowerShell (or Terminal) and press Enter. Use the normal one, not “Run as administrator”. The line ends in >, for example PS C:\Users\anna>.


Press Ctrl+Alt+T, or open Terminal from the applications menu. The line ends in $.





Step 2: Where am I, and what is here?
Type each command and press Enter.
pwd
ls
pwd should print your home folder. ls should list names you recognise from your file browser: Desktop, Documents, Downloads and so on.


Step 3: Make the course folder and go into it
mkdir agentic-course
ls
cd agentic-course
pwd
After mkdir, the second ls should show agentic-course in the list. After cd, the prompt changes, and pwd shows a path ending in agentic-course.






Tip



Use Tab: type cd agen and press Tab. The terminal completes the name. Use the up arrow to bring back a command you typed before.


If your institution asks you to keep work files in a particular place (for example a OneDrive folder), make agentic-course there instead and cd to it. Avoid the Desktop.


Step 4: Open the folder in your file browser



macOS
Windows
Linux




open .
explorer .
xdg-open .



An empty folder called agentic-course opens. Place it next to the terminal window. You will watch it in the next steps.


What you should see on your system

macOSWindowsLinux









Command
What you see




pwd
/Users/anna (your user name)


ls
Applications  Desktop  Documents  Downloads  ...


mkdir agentic-course
nothing: silence means it worked


cd agentic-course
nothing, but the prompt now ends in agentic-course %


pwd
/Users/anna/agentic-course


open .
a Finder window showing the empty folder


claude / codex
the agent’s welcome screen, maybe a question about trusting the folder



macOS may ask “Terminal would like to access files in your Documents folder” if you work in Documents or Desktop. Another reason to use ~/agentic-course.









Command
What you see




pwd
a small table: Path, ----, C:\Users\anna


ls (or dir)
a table with columns Mode, LastWriteTime, Length, Name


mkdir agentic-course
a short table describing the new folder (this is normal)


cd agentic-course
nothing, but the prompt now reads PS C:\Users\anna\agentic-course>


pwd
C:\Users\anna\agentic-course (in the same small table)


explorer .
a File Explorer window showing the empty folder


claude / codex
the agent’s welcome screen, maybe a question about trusting the folder



On many Windows computers, Documents and Desktop are inside OneDrive (C:\Users\anna\OneDrive\Documents). That is why we use a folder directly in your home folder.









Command
What you see




pwd
/home/anna


ls
Desktop  Documents  Downloads  ...


mkdir agentic-course
nothing: silence means it worked


cd agentic-course
nothing, but the prompt now shows ~/agentic-course


pwd
/home/anna/agentic-course


xdg-open .
your file manager showing the empty folder


claude / codex
the agent’s welcome screen, maybe a question about trusting the folder








Step 5: Start the agent in the course folder
Check with pwd that you are in agentic-course. Then start one of the agents (or both, one after the other):



Claude Code
Codex




claude
codex



If it asks whether you trust this folder, answer yes: it is your own, empty folder.


Step 6: Make the agent ask before it changes anything

Claude CodeCodex


Look at the line below the prompt box. If it says that auto mode or accept edits is on, press Shift+Tab until it says manual mode on. (Recent versions start in auto mode. One press usually takes you to Manual.)


Type /status and press Enter. Look for the approval and sandbox settings. Then type /permissions and choose Read Only, so that Codex asks before it writes a file. (In a plain folder like this one, Codex may already be in Read Only.)





Step 7: Look at the commands available







Claude Code
Codex




Type /help and press Enter. Close it with Esc.
Type / and look at the list that appears. Press Esc to close it.



Find the commands that exit, that start a new conversation, and that show the status. Write them down; the names change between versions.


Step 8: Ask the agent to create a file
Type this into the prompt box:
Create a file called notes.md in this folder with exactly three lines:
Course: Introduction to agentic AI
Folder: the full path of this folder
Today I learned: to read the terminal before I approve anything
What to look for: the agent should ask for permission before it writes the file. Read the request:

What: is it creating notes.md, and nothing else?
Where: is the file inside agentic-course?
How long: choose the plain Yes (once), not the “don’t ask again” or “allow for this session” option.

Look at the file browser. notes.md appears in the folder. Double-click it to open it in a text editor (if your computer asks which program to use, choose a text editor such as TextEdit or Notepad).
If the agent did not ask, check the mode again (Step 6). The file is still fine; this time you just skipped the practice.


Step 9: Say no, and tell the agent what to do instead
Type:
Make a folder called archive and move notes.md into it.
The agent will probably ask to run a command such as mkdir archive or mv notes.md archive/, possibly both in one line.

When it asks to move notes.md, answer No, and add an instruction:

Claude Code: highlight No, press Tab, type Keep notes.md where it is. Only make the archive folder. and press Enter.
Codex: choose the option to decline and tell Codex what to do differently, then type the same sentence.

When it then asks to run only mkdir archive, answer Yes.



Step 10: Ask the agent to explain a command
Type:
Which command would you use to delete the archive folder?
Explain in plain words what it does and whether it can be undone. Do not run it.
What to look for: a command such as rm -r archive (or Remove-Item on Windows), an explanation that it deletes the folder and everything in it, and a clear statement that it does not go to the wastebasket. Nothing should run.
Now ask about the very first command you typed today:
What does the command ls -la show that plain ls does not?


Step 11 (optional): Check which software is installed
Later units need R, Python and git. Ask, without installing anything:
Which of R, Python and git are installed on this computer, and which versions?
Only check. Do not install anything.
The agent will want to run commands like R --version, python3 --version and git --version. These only look, so Yes is safe. Write down what is missing; installation is covered when a unit first needs it.


Step 12: Exit the agent



Claude Code
Codex




/exit (or Ctrl+C twice)
/exit or /quit (or Ctrl+C)



You are back at the normal terminal prompt. Type pwd: you are still in agentic-course. Type ls: you should see archive and notes.md.
If you have both tools, repeat Steps 5 to 12 with the other one. Ask it to add a fourth line to notes.md instead of creating the file again.


Check the result
Do not take the agent’s word for it. Check each point yourself:

In the file browser, agentic-course contains notes.md and an empty folder archive. notes.md is not inside archive (you said no).
Open notes.md in a text editor. It has exactly three lines (four if you used both tools). The second line shows the full path of your course folder, and that path matches what pwd printed in the terminal.
In the terminal, after exiting the agent, pwd ends in agentic-course and ls lists the same two names as the file browser.
You can say, in one sentence each, what pwd, ls, cd, cd .., mkdir, mv and rm do.
You wrote down the names of the commands that exit, start a new conversation, and show the status in the tool(s) you use.

If something does not match, that is useful: ask the agent “Why is notes.md in archive?” (or whatever is wrong) and compare its answer with what you see.

title: Exercise: watch an agent work
section: Before you start
text:
Before you start

Have the lecture slides at hand, especially the slides on the agent loop and the two-question grid.
Have something to write on: a text document, a spreadsheet or paper. You keep your answers.
Optional: look at the example data, seedlings.csv. It is synthetic (made up by a script), so nothing in it is real or personal. It has 192 rows: 24 pea seedlings (8 each under low, medium and high light), height in mm measured every second day from day 0 to day 14.

title: Exercise: watch an agent work
section: Worked example: read an annotated agent session
text:
Worked example: read an annotated agent session
Below is a full session in which an agent turns seedlings.csv into a plot with an R script. It is written out in the style of Claude Code in a terminal; a Codex session looks much the same, with slightly different symbols and wording. The data, the final script and both plots are real. Your own sessions, once you have installed a tool, will look different in the details: agents do not give the same answer twice.
Read the whole session once without stopping. Then read it again with the questions in the next section.







How to read this. Lines starting with > are what the person typed. Lines starting with ● are the agent: either something it says, or a tool it uses (Read, Write, Update, Bash). Lines starting with ⎿ show the result of that tool. The numbers in the margin ([1], [2], …) are there so you can refer to steps in your answers.




[1] The person gives the task
The folder seedling-project contains one file, seedlings.csv. The person starts the agent in that folder and types:
> Make a line plot of mean seedling height per light treatment over time,
  with error bars. There are three treatments. Use an R script so I can
  rerun it, and save the figure as growth_plot.png.


[2] The agent looks at the data
● I'll start by looking at the data file.

● Read(seedlings.csv)
  ⎿ Read 193 lines
    "plant_id","treatment","day","height_mm"
    "l01","low",0,12.2
    "l01","low",2,13.2
    "l01","low",4,20.1
    "l01","low",6,22.3
    "l01","low",8,26
    … +187 lines

● The file is in long format: one row per plant per day, with columns
  plant_id, treatment, day (0 to 14, every second day) and height_mm.
  Plan:
    1. Write plot_growth.R: read the CSV, compute mean and standard error
       of height per treatment and day, draw one line per treatment.
    2. Run it and look at the figure.


[3] The agent writes a script
● Write(plot_growth.R)
  ⎿ Wrote 19 lines to plot_growth.R
     1 library(ggplot2)
     2
     3 d <- read.csv("seedlings.csv")
     4
     5 summ <- aggregate(height_mm ~ treatment + day, data = d,
     6   FUN = function(x) c(mean = mean(x), se = sd(x) / sqrt(length(x))))
     7 summ <- do.call(data.frame, summ)
     8 names(summ) <- c("treatment", "day", "mean", "se")
     9
    10 p <- ggplot(summ, aes(day, mean, colour = treatment)) +
    11   geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
    12   geom_point(size = 2) +
    13   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - se, ymax = mean + se), width = 0.3) +
    14   labs(x = "Day", y = "Seedling height (mm)", colour = "Light",
    15        title = "Seedling growth under three light levels") +
    16   theme_minimal(base_size = 14)
    17
    18 ggsave("growth_plot.png", p, width = 7, height = 4.5, dpi = 150)
    19


[4] The agent asks for permission to run it
● Bash(Rscript plot_growth.R)

  ╭─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
  │ Bash command                                                    │
  │                                                                 │
  │   Rscript plot_growth.R                                         │
  │   Run the plotting script to create growth_plot.png             │
  │                                                                 │
  │ Do you want to proceed?                                         │
  │ ❯ 1. Yes                                                        │
  │   2. Yes, and don't ask again for Rscript commands in this      │
  │      folder                                                     │
  │   3. No, and tell Claude what to do differently (esc)           │
  ╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
The person reads the command, sees that it only runs the script that was just written, and chooses 2.
  ⎿ (no output)


[5] The agent looks at its own result and notices a problem
● The script ran without errors. Let me check the figure.

● Read(growth_plot.png)
  ⎿ Read image (63 KB)



What the agent saw: the first version of the plot.


● The legend shows four groups: "high", "High", "low" and "medium". You
  said there are three treatments, so "High" and "high" are probably the
  same treatment typed two ways. Let me count the labels and check for
  missing values before changing anything.

● Bash(Rscript -e 'd <- read.csv("seedlings.csv"); print(table(d$treatment));
       print(d[is.na(d$height_mm), ]); print(unique(d$plant_id[d$treatment == "High"]))')
  ⎿
      high   High    low medium
        48     16     64     64
       plant_id treatment day height_mm
    86      m03    medium  10        NA
    [1] "h07" "h08"

● Findings:
  - 16 rows (plants h07 and h08) are labelled "High"; the other high-light
    plants use "high". Their plant IDs start with h like the others, so
    they look like the same treatment.
  - One height value is missing (plant m03, day 10).
  - The first script did not say anything about the missing value:
    aggregate() silently drops it.
  I'll make the labels lower case, report the missing value explicitly,
  and put the treatments in a sensible order (low, medium, high).


[6] The agent fixes the script
● Update(plot_growth.R)
  ⎿ Updated plot_growth.R with 11 additions
     3   d <- read.csv("seedlings.csv")
     4 +
     5 + # Treatment labels were typed inconsistently ("High" and "high"):
     6 + # make them lower case so they form one group.
     7 + d$treatment <- tolower(trimws(d$treatment))
     8 + d$treatment <- factor(d$treatment, levels = c("low", "medium", "high"))
     9 +
    10 + # One measurement is missing; leave it out of the means.
    11 + n_missing <- sum(is.na(d$height_mm))
    12 + d <- d[!is.na(d$height_mm), ]
    13 + message("Rows with missing height removed: ", n_missing)
    14
(The agent also added a line that prints how many plants there are per treatment, a subtitle, and fixed colours. The final script is in data/plot_growth.R.)


[7] The agent runs it again and checks again
● Bash(Rscript plot_growth.R)
  ⎿ Rows with missing height removed: 1
    Plants per treatment: low 8, medium 8, high 8

● Read(growth_plot.png)
  ⎿ Read image (62 KB)



What the agent saw the second time: the final plot.




[8] The agent reports back
● Done. growth_plot.png now shows three treatments (low, medium, high),
  mean height ± 1 standard error, 8 plants per treatment.

  Files:
  - plot_growth.R: the script (rerun with: Rscript plot_growth.R)
  - growth_plot.png: the figure

  Decisions I made that you should check:
  1. I treated "High" (plants h07, h08) as the same treatment as "high".
     If they were a separate condition, tell me and I'll plot them apart.
  2. One missing height (plant m03, day 10) was left out, so that point
     is the mean of 7 plants, not 8.
  3. Error bars are standard errors, not standard deviations.


Questions on the session
Write short answers. Refer to steps by their number, for example “in [5]”.
Q1. Reading. In which steps did the agent read something, and what did it read? (Hint: it read more than the CSV.)
Q2. Permission. Where did the agent ask for permission, and what exactly did it want to do? The agent ran Rscript three times in total, but asked only once. Why? Would you have chosen option 1 or option 2, and why?
Q3. Checking. What did the agent check on its own initiative, without being asked? What made it suspicious in the first place?
Q4. Decisions. List the decisions the agent made without asking you. For each one, say whether you are happy for an agent to make that kind of decision alone, or whether it should have stopped and asked.
Q5. Your own checks. You are the teacher who ran this lab. Name three concrete checks you would make before you show this plot to students. Be specific: what would you open, what would you compare, what number would you expect?
Q6. Chat versus agent. Imagine doing the same task in a chat window. Which of steps [2] to [8] would you have had to do yourself?


Check the result
You do not have to trust the plot either. Do at least two of these checks; they need only a spreadsheet program.

Count the labels. Open seedlings.csv in Excel, LibreOffice or Numbers. Filter or sort the treatment column. Do you see 48 rows of high and 16 of High, as the agent said in step [5]? Which plants are the High ones?
Recompute one point by hand. Filter to low and day = 0. Take the mean of the 8 heights. The plot shows the first low point at a little over 10 mm. Do you agree? (Use the spreadsheet’s AVERAGE function.)
Find the missing value. Find the row with an empty height_mm. Is it the plant and day the agent reported in step [8]?
Look at the “High” plants. Compare the day 14 heights of h07 and h08 with the other six high-light plants. Are they similar, or do they stand out? What would that make you ask the student who typed them?







Model answers (open after you have tried)





Q1. [2] read seedlings.csv; [5] read growth_plot.png (it looked at its own figure) and read the CSV again via a small R command; [7] read growth_plot.png again. In [6] the agent edited plot_growth.R, which means it had the file’s contents in front of it.
Q2. Only in [4], to run Rscript plot_growth.R. The person chose option 2 (“don’t ask again for Rscript commands in this folder”), so the later Rscript runs in [5] and [7] went ahead without a prompt. Option 2 is reasonable here because every Rscript call stays inside a folder of example data. With your own data, option 1 (ask every time) is the safer choice until you trust the setup. Note that in Codex the default limits are different: it usually runs commands inside the project folder without asking and asks before going outside it. Terminal survival kit covers how to set these limits.
Q3. It looked at the figure, saw four groups where the task said three, counted rows per label, looked for missing values, and listed which plants carried the odd label. After the fix it printed the number of plants per treatment and looked at the figure again. What made it suspicious: the person had written “There are three treatments” in the prompt. Without that sentence, a four-line plot would have looked fine to the agent.
Q4. (a) Merging High into high. (b) Dropping the missing value. (c) Using standard errors rather than standard deviations. (d) Choosing the order and colours of the treatments. (c) and (d) are fine to decide alone, as long as they are reported. (a) changes the meaning of the data and arguably should have been a question (“Should I merge these?”) rather than a decision reported afterwards. A prompt can ask for this: “If the data disagree with what I said, stop and ask before changing anything.”
Q5. Good answers are concrete, for example: count the labels in the CSV (48 + 16 = 64 high rows); recompute one plotted mean by hand (low, day 0: mean 10.55 mm); check that h07 and h08 really were under the same lamp (their day 14 heights, 59.8 and 67.5 mm, are among the tallest, which could mean a different lamp, a different student measuring, or chance); check that the y-axis unit (mm) matches how heights were measured; check that “8 plants per treatment” in the subtitle is honest given the missing value; check that the error bars are what you would show students (SE or SD).
Q6. In a chat window you would have done almost all of it: describe the file (the chat cannot see it), copy the script into a file, run it, look at the plot, notice the fourth group yourself, find the cause, paste it back, copy the corrected script, run it again. The agent did [2] to [7]; you would still do the judging in [8].





Optional: run the same session yourself, after the next unit
Once you have installed a tool in Accounts and installation, you can try this yourself. Make a new empty folder, copy seedlings.csv into it, start the agent in that folder and give it the same prompt.

Claude CodeCodex


Start it in the folder by typing claude, then paste:
Make a line plot of mean seedling height per light treatment over time,
with error bars. There are three treatments. Use an R script so I can
rerun it, and save the figure as growth_plot.png.


Start it in the folder by typing codex, then paste:
Make a line plot of mean seedling height per light treatment over time,
with error bars. There are three treatments. Use an R script so I can
rerun it, and save the figure as growth_plot.png.



You need R with the ggplot2 package. If you do not have it yet, wait until Terminal survival kit, where the agent helps you install it. Expect a different session: perhaps the agent asks about High before merging, perhaps it does not notice at all. Either way, do the checks above.

Try it on something of yours: sort five chores
You choose your own project at the end of Part 1, in Privacy, ethics and safety. This task prepares that choice. It uses no data at all, only a description of your work, so it is privacy-safe. Do not paste anything from these chores into a chat or an agent yet.
Step 1. List five chores. Think of the last month. Write down five tasks from your own job that took time, involved files, and felt like they were not the core of your work. Write one line each, concrete enough that a colleague would know what you mean. Examples:

“Merge the exam results from four teaching assistants’ spreadsheets into one.”
“Redraw Figure 3 of the manuscript with the new batch included.”
“Get the sample size from each of the 30 papers in my review into one table.”
“Rename 400 microscope images from the plate map.”
“Put the reading list, schedule and slides for my seminar course on one page.”

Step 2. Rate each chore on two questions.

How easy is it to check the result? Easy: you could tell right from wrong in a few minutes (a known total, a figure you know well, a page you can look at). Hard: checking would take nearly as long as doing it, or you are not sure what right looks like.
How sensitive is the data? Low: public, synthetic or your own non-personal material. High: personal data about students, patients or staff, unpublished data under agreement, anything your university restricts.
